title: 第五章 实践中的人民主权
originalTitle: 5 The Sovereignty of the People in Practice

zh: 在论证的这一阶段，我们对拜占庭共和国的描绘
包含以下要素：(a) 一个为公共领域的运作设定共和规范的概念（
）；(b) 皇帝们自身的纲领性承认，即其职位的目的在于增进臣民的福祉与共和国的利益；(c) 人民（事实上是整个
，通过其代表）对新皇帝欢呼仪式的参与，以便依照那些共和规范授予他正当性（但很少参与他的选举）；以及 (d) 若干“民众行动”的时刻，即人民在正式制度框架之外把政治领域掌握到自己手中。事实上，人民有权参与的唯一制度就是那些欢呼，而许多学者认为，那不过是罗马惯例留下的一点陈旧遗迹。
en: At this stage in the argument our portrait of the Byzantine Republic contains
the following elements: (a) a concept (the

) that posits republican norms for the operation of the public sphere; (b) programmatic acknowledgments by the emperors themselves that the purpose of their office was to promote the welfare of their subjects and the good of the republic; (c) ritual participation of the people (in fact, the entire

through its representatives) in the acclamation of a new emperor, in order to confer legitimacy upon him according to those republican norms (but rarely in his election); and (d) a few moments of “mob action,” when the people took the political sphere into their own hands outside the framework of formal institutions. In fact, the only institution in which the people had the right to participate were those acclamations, which, many scholars believe, were an antiquated shadow of Roman practices.

zh: 即便这些也已说明了很多，并为重新评估拜占庭政治领域提供了基础。然而，共和主义的论证还可以推进得更远。我们必须首先搁置本领域对国家正式制度的执念，因为除了新皇帝的欢呼这一部分例外，这些制度几乎全都属于
本身，即它们是皇权行使（司法、军事、财政等）的各个方面。但
与

并非可以互换。拜占庭的共和性质，主要取决于这些制度在怎样的观念框架内运作。例如，并不存在一种公法结构来界定共和国内部行使君主权力的目的与范围；那是皇帝与臣民凭借身为共和国股东这一身份而彼此知晓并协商的东西。教育皇帝认识其权力目的的并非任何成文“宪法”，但他们却一贯宣称其权力在于服务共和国。没有制度为皇帝设定正式限制，但他们若越过共识的界限就要自担风险。没有法律规范继承的方式，而在这里人民拥有最终发言权。总之，人民的真实权力是法外的、处于制度运作之外的。事实上，当人民干预时，那往往采取中止法律权威的形式，其间有些人甚至趁机犯下罪行。但这些非制度性干预的目的，是确立一种新的法律权威，或恢复一种岌岌可危的法律权威。拜占庭在两种状态之间摇摆：一是皇帝作为“有生命的法律”而统治，一种永久例外状态，其稳定仅以皇帝选择尊重共和国规范为限；二是人民的法外主权，在缺乏固定制度的情况下，它往往以暴力和革命的方式被宣示。恰恰因为它能够造就和撤销皇帝的正当性，它运作于帝国法律的领域之外。
en: Even this is saying a lot already, and provides the basis for a reevaluation of the Byzantine political sphere. The argument for republicanism, however, can be taken much further. We must first set aside the field’s fixation on the formal institutions of the state, for, with the partial exception of the acclamations of new emperors, these were almost all part of the
itself, that is, they were aspects of the exercise of imperial authority ( judicial, military, fiscal, etc.). But the
and the

were not interchangeable. The republicanism of Byzantium was a function not so much of institutions as of the ideological context in which those institutions operated. For instance, there was no structure of public law that defined the purpose and scope of the exercise of monarchical power within the republic; that was something that emperors and subjects knew and negotiated between them by virtue of being shareholders in the republic. It was not any written “constitution” that educated emperors as to the purpose of their power, yet they consistently proclaimed that it was to serve the republic. No institutions set formal limits on the emperors, yet they crossed the limits of consensus at their peril. There were no laws that regulated the manner of the succession, and here the people had the final say. In sum, the real power of the people was extralegal and outside the operation of institutions. In fact, when the people intervened, that often took the form of a suspension of legal authority, during which some even took the opportunity to commit criminal acts. But the purpose of these noninstitutional interventions was to institute a new legal authority, or to restore one that was in jeopardy. Byzantium oscillated between the “animate law” of the emperor, a state of permanent exception that was stable only insofar as the emperor chose to respect the norms of the republic, and the extralegal sovereignty of the people, which, in the absence of fixed institutions, was often asserted in a violent and revolutionary way. Precisely because it could make and unmake imperial legitimacy, it operated beyond the sphere of imperial law.

zh: 民众干预的模式
en: Patterns of Popular Intervention

zh: 本章将通过考察人民宣示主权权利的一系列情境，为理论论证赋予历史分量。米海尔五世（Michael V）的覆灭并非反常现象。人民经常干预多种类型的争议——政治的、宗教的、王朝的——哪怕只是为了表达不满，而皇帝若想保住皇位就必须留意。以下选取的事件旨在展示民众干预的叙事如何展开、其底层前提为何。我把这里的选取限定为人民是不满之主要推动者的情形。我避开了那些由竞技场党派（亦称
）主导行动的情形，以免卷入关于它们的作用及其在多大程度上代表人民的争论。
我也把存在阴谋或叛军行动的情形留到本章后面一节讨论，即便人民在危机的解决中起了决定性作用；这类事件将要求我们对人民主权的对这些情况下的人民主权作更细致的说明。当人民施展其集体力量时，他们既能废黜一位皇帝，也能阻止一位叛将夺取皇位。决定因素是两人相对的“声望”，因此这将引向对拜占庭舆论的讨论。
en: This chapter will give historical weight to the theoretical argument by considering a range of environments in which the people asserted sovereign rights. The downfall of Michael V was not an aberration. The people intervened regularly in many types of controversies—political, religious, and dynastic—even if only to register their discontent, and emperors had to pay heed if they wished to stay on the throne. The following selection of episodes aims to show how the narrative of popular intervention played out and what its underlying premises were. I have restricted the selection here to instances when the people were the primary agent of discontent. I have avoided those in which the racing factions (also called the
) dominated the action, in order to stay clear of the debate over their role and the degree to which they represented the people.

I have also deferred to a later section of this chapter discussion of cases where there was a conspiracy or rebel army in motion, even if the people played a decisive role in the resolution of the crisis; such events will require us to nuance the argument for popular sovereignty. When the people flexed their collective muscle, they could either depose an emperor or block a rebel from seizing the throne. The deciding factor was the relative “popularity” of the two men, so this will lead to a discussion of public opinion in Byzantium.

zh: 我的目的是恢复这些干预的
维度，表明它们不只是躁动群众（“群氓”）就娱乐等非政治问题发动的暴乱。我还想提请注意皇帝如何回应这些干预：除少数例外，他们屈服于人民的要求，或对此别无选择，或谦卑地请求宽恕，以拖延时间或重建正当性。这正是我们在一个共和式君主制中所预期的。若皇位被理解为基础于绝对原则、尤其是神权原则，那就不是我们所预期的。只有一位皇帝曾成功反击一场协调一致的起义：查士丁尼。
我们从阿纳斯塔修斯（Anastasios）开始，其即位的情形及其所受的约束我们在第4章已见证。
en: My purpose is to restore the

dimension of these interventions, to show that they were not just riots by the restless masses (“the mob”) over nonpolitical issues, such as entertainments. I wish also to draw attention to how emperors responded to these interventions: with few exceptions, they submitted to the demands of the people, or had no choice in the matter, or humbly asked for forgiveness, to play for time or reestablish their legitimacy. This is what we would expect in a republican monarchy. It is not what we would expect if the throne was understood to be based on absolute, especially theocratic, principles. Only one emperor ever struck back successfully against a concerted uprising, Justinian.
We begin with Anastasios, the circumstances and terms of whose accession we witnessed in Chapter 4.

zh: • 511年，一场教义争议使皇帝阿纳斯塔修斯与牧首马其顿尼乌斯（Makedonios）对立。同情马其顿尼乌斯的史家塞奥多罗斯·阿纳格诺斯特斯（Theodoros Anagnostes）可能亲见此事。他说，包括妇女、儿童和修道院长在内的庞大人群（πλῆθος ἄπειρον）涌起保卫牧首，并侮辱皇帝，称他为摩尼教徒、“不配享有
”。塞奥多罗斯想让我们相信，由于这场抗议，阿纳斯塔修斯“出于对人群的恐惧”而改变了主意，并邀请马其顿尼乌斯回宫；沿途牧首甚至受到卫队的欢呼。
当然，民众在这个问题上是有分歧的，抗议也并未推翻政权，但这部史料希望读者相信：只要阿纳斯塔修斯不尊重他们的意愿，他在共同体眼中就是 在法理上（
）不具正当性的，或至少可能如此。宗教抗议在这里以共和政治的形式表达自身。阿纳斯塔修斯最终以牧首称他为异端、并据称阴谋反对他为由将其废黜。但在此之前，他召集了卫队队长和宫廷的
，要求他们宣誓效忠于他和
，随后向军队发放赏赐，并在城门和港口设岗。
en: • In 511, a doctrinal controversy pitted the emperor Anastasios against the patriarch Makedonios. A source favorable to Makedonios, Theodoros Anagnostes, who may have been present, claims that a vast multitude (πλῆθος ἄπειρον), including women, children, and abbots, surged to the patriarch’s defense and insulted the emperor, calling him a Manichaean and “unworthy of the

” Theodoros would have us believe that because of this protest Anastasios changed his mind “out of his fear of the crowd” and invited Makedonios back to the palace; along the way, the patriarch was even acclaimed by the guard.
Certainly, the populace was divided on this issue and the protests did not topple the regime, but this source wants its readers to believe that Anastasios was

illegitimate in the eyes of the community, or potentially so, for as long as he did not respect their wishes. Religious protest was here expressing itself in the form of republican politics. Anastasios eventually deposed the patriarch for calling him a heretic and allegedly plotting against him. But before doing so, he summoned the captains of the guard and the
of the court and required them to swear an oath of loyalty to him and the
gave largess to the army, and set guards at the gates and harbors.

zh: • 512年，阿纳斯塔修斯的统治又因一场宗教问题上的民众抗议而动摇。抗议者高呼“给罗曼尼亚一位新皇帝（ἄλλον βασιλέα τῇ Ῥωμανίᾳ）”，并在焚毁不受欢迎的前都城长官马里诺斯（Marinos）的宅邸后拥立阿雷奥宾杜斯（Areobindos）。阿雷奥宾杜斯逃走了，但阿纳斯塔修斯不戴冠冕出现在赛马场，表示愿意退位，这才平息了人群。
当人民要他重新戴上冠冕时，他们是在象征性地重新授予他皇权——那正是他们最初在491年授予他的。
以悔罪之姿出现在赛马场并愿意开启谈判，是皇帝对此类局面的标准回应，正如我们在米海尔五世（1042年）身上所见、并在本章将屡见不鲜。
en: • In 512, Anastasios’s reign was rocked by another popular protest over a religious question. The protesters were chanting, “A new emperor for Romanía (ἄλλον βασιλέα τῇ Ῥωμανίᾳ),” and they declared for Areobindos after burning the house of the unpopular ex-prefect Marinos. Areobindos fled but Anastasios appeared in the hippodrome without his crown and offered to abdicate, which calmed the crowd.
When the people told him to put his crown back on, they were symbolically reinvesting him with imperial authority, which they had originally given to him in 491.
A contrite appearance in the hippodrome and a desire to open negotiations were a standard imperial response to such situations, as we saw with Michael V (in 1042) and will see often in this chapter.

zh: • 532年，都城人民试图在罗马史上最暴烈的起义之一——尼卡暴动——中推翻皇帝查士丁尼的政权。诚然，它由党派与城市当局的冲突引爆，但很快随着民众带着对政权的不满加入而具有了普遍性质，他们纵火焚烧
（火势迅速蔓延）。应当指出，元老院多数或全部成员最终加入了起义，但并未策划它；而人群先后拥立的对立皇帝——先是逃走的普罗布斯（Probos，人群曾高呼 Πρόβον βασιλέα τῇ ῾Ρωμανίᾳ），然后是许帕提乌斯（Hypatios，也是阿纳斯塔修斯的侄子）——都不情愿，尽管许帕提乌斯后来动了心。是人民主动在赛马场拥立他为皇帝，这表明他们相信自己有权这样做。没有史料反驳这一信念。
查士丁尼作出让步以安抚人群，罢免了被要求撤职的不受欢迎官员，并出现在赛马场与民众谈判。当一切似乎都已无望时，他考虑出逃，直到据普罗科匹乌斯（Prokopios）记载，他被妻子塞奥多拉（Theodora）鼓舞而反击——史家通常把她描绘为自由罗马
之方式与秩序的死敌。
无论如何，这是拜占庭历史上唯一一次失败的人民起义。
en: • In 532, the people of the City attempted to take down the regime of the emperor Justinian in one of the most violent uprisings in Roman history, the Nika riots. To be sure, it was sparked by a confrontation between the factions and the urban authorities, but it soon acquired a general character as the populace joined in with its grievances against the regime, setting fire to the

(which quickly spread). It should be noted that most or all of the senate eventually joined the uprising but had not orchestrated it, and the rival emperors proclaimed by the crowd, first Probos who fled (the crowd had chanted Πρόβον βασιλέα τῇ ῾Ρωμανίᾳ), then Hypatios (also a nephew of Anastasios) were unwilling, though Hypatios warmed to it. It was the people, on their own initiative, who proclaimed him emperor in the hippodrome, which indicates that they believed that they had the right to do this. No source counters this belief.

Justinian made concessions to pacify the crowd, dismissing unpopular officials whose deposition had been demanded and appearing in the hippodrome to negotiate with the populace. When all seemed lost, he considered flight until, according to Prokopios, he was emboldened to fight back by his wife Theodora, whom the historian generally presents as an enemy of the modes and orders of the free Roman
At any rate, this was the only insurrection of the people in Byzantine history that failed.

zh: • 577年，来自东部城市的异教徒因举行邪恶仪式而在君士坦丁堡受审，但据信他们因法官受贿而被释放。人民开始低语抗议，很快大量聚集，高呼“挖出法官的骨头！”“挖出异教徒的骨头！”十万人响应这些呼喊。他们砸毁了举行审判的宫殿，打破监狱释放囚犯，并销毁了
中的档案。皇帝（提比略二世，Tiberios II）设法平息了他们的情绪；一份记述指出抗议者此前也在谴责他。随后他惩处了暴动的一些据称首要分子，但也重审并定罪了原先被宣告无罪的异教徒，导致一场反异教徒清洗。
en: • In 577, pagans from eastern cities were put on trial in Constantinople for performing nefarious rites, but, it was believed, they were let go because the judges had been bribed. The people began to murmur and protest and soon gather in large numbers, chanting, “Dig up the judges’ bones!” and “Dig up the pagans’ bones!” A hundred thousand people rallied to these cries. They smashed the palace in which the trials had been held, broke open the prisons and set the prisoners free, and destroyed the records in the

The emperor (Tiberios II) managed to calm their spirits; one account notes that the protesters had been denouncing him as well. He then punished some of the alleged ringleaders of the riot, but also retried and convicted the pagans who had originally been acquitted, leading to an antipagan purge.

zh: • 598年，将军科门提奥洛斯（Kommentiolos）被阿瓦尔人击败，伤亡惨重。据信他故意把士兵引向死亡以惩罚他们，理由在各记述中说法不一，甚至包括皇帝莫里斯（Maurikios）曾指示他这样做。色雷斯的军队致信要求调查他。都城爆发激烈暴动，迫使皇帝任命一个调查委员会（指控被驳斥，将军获重新任命）。
en: • In 598, the general Kommentiolos was defeated in battle by the Avars and took many casualties. It was believed that he had deliberately led his soldiers to their deaths to punish them for reasons that are given variously in different accounts, including even that the emperor Maurikios had instructed him to do so. The armies in Thrace sent letters demanding that he be investigated. A fierce riot broke out in the City, which forced the emperor to appoint a commission to investigate (the charge was refuted and the general was reappointed).

zh: • 在与波斯战争的低谷，大约在610年代末，希拉克略（Herakleios）绝望地提议迁都迦太基，但“市民们竭力反对”，牧首让他在祭坛上宣誓不离都城。
en: • At the lowest point in the war with Persia, probably in the late 610s, Herakleios proposed in despair to move the capital to Carthage, but “the citizens opposed this as best they could” and the patriarch made him swear on the altar that he would not leave the City.

zh: • 641年，希拉克略死后，他不受欢迎的遗孀（兼侄女）马蒂娜（Martina）召集牧首、职官与君士坦丁堡人民；宣布希拉克略的遗嘱，即其子君士坦丁（Konstantinos）与希拉克略（赫拉克洛纳斯，Heraklonas）应被拥立为共帝；并要求她以奥古斯塔（Augusta）身份获得最高皇位。但人民中有人向她喊话，说她应满足于皇帝母亲的地位。她也不应接见外国使节：“愿上帝禁止罗马
落到这般地步。”随后他们欢呼两位皇帝，却不欢呼她。
我们无法知道那次会议上谁说了什么、人民如何集体表达意见。可能是一些显贵在发言，但未必：人民很可能有自己的代言人。然而重要的是，“人民”被集体描绘为拥有最终发言权，无论实际说话的是谁。唯有他们有权批准此类决定。马蒂娜撤回了她的要求。
en: • In 641, after the death of Herakleios, his widow (and niece), Martina, who was unpopular, assembled the patriarch, the magistrates, and the people of Constantinople; announced Herakleios’s will that his sons Konstantinos and Herakleios (Heraklonas) be proclaimed co-emperors; and asked that she, as Augusta, be given the senior imperial rank. But some of the people cried out to her that she should be content with the rank of mother of the emperors. Nor was she to receive foreign embassies: “May God forbid that the Roman
should come to such a pass.” They then acclaimed the emperors, but not her.

We cannot know who said what at that meeting or how the people collectively expressed their opinion. Possibly some of the notables were doing the speaking, though not necessarily: the people may well have had their own spokesmen. What matters, however, is that “the people” collectively are depicted as having the final say, regardless of who was actually doing the talking. Only they had the authority to ratify such decisions. Martina withdrew her claim.

zh: • 据彼得·哈特利（Peter Hatlie），“整个〔七〕世纪期间，反对教会与政府的大规模民众示威仍周期性发生，包括世纪初反对削减面包配给的抗议、世纪中叶‘元老院与都城’对牧首皮尔霍斯（Pyrrhos）的谴责，以及668年与695年君士坦斯二世（Konstas II）与查士丁尼二世各自被废前对他们发泄的憎恶。所有这些在君士坦丁堡街头、赛马场与大教堂发生的示威，值得注意的是，都没有任何关于修士以个人或群体身份参与的报道”（他为此全部引了史料）。
en: • According to Peter Hatlie, “mass popular manifestations against Church and government continued to occur periodically over the course of the [seventh] century, including protests against the reduction in bread rations early in the century, the denunciations of patriarch Pyrrhos by ‘Senate and City’ at mid-century, and the odium vented against Konstas II and Justinian II prior to their respective dethronements in 668 and 695. All of these demonstrations in Constantinople’s streets, hippodrome, and Great Church took place, remarkably, without any reported participation by monks on an individual or group basis” (he cites sources for all of this).

zh: • 1044年，君士坦丁九世（Konstantinos IX）正以盛大行列前往教堂，有人喊道：“我们不要斯克勒赖娜（Skleraina，他的情妇）做皇后，也不要我们生于紫室的母亲佐伊（Zoe）与塞奥多拉为她而死。”于是人民暴动，几乎杀死皇帝。直到两位皇后现身他们才平静下来，皇帝逃回宫中。这是1042年废黜米海尔五世的后续。
en: • In 1044, Konstantinos IX was on his way to church in a grand procession when someone called out, “We do not want Skleraina [his mistress] as an empress, nor do we want our mothers, Zoe and Theodora who were born in the purple, to die for her sake.” Whereupon the people rioted and came close to killing the emperor. They calmed down only when the empresses appeared, and the emperor fled back to the palace. This was a follow-up to the deposition of Michael V in 1042.

zh: • 1197年，阿莱克修斯三世·安格洛斯（Alexios III Angelos）强征一种“德意志税”，实质上是为免遭西方进攻而缴纳的保护费。他召集都城全体人民、元老院、教士与各行业——很可能在赛马场——请各方出钱。 但很快他就看出自己一无所成，他的话不过是空谈。多数人认为这些沉重而反常的勒令完全不可容忍，于是喧嚷抗议，眼看就要起事。皇帝被一些人指责挥霍公共财富（τὰ κοινὰ）、把行省分给他的亲属——而那些人都无能而昏聩——于是迅速放弃了提议，几乎等于说这主意不是他提出的。
en: • In 1197, Alexios III Angelos imposed a “German tax,” basically protection money to stave off a western attack. He assembled all the people of the City, the senate, the clergy, and the trades, probably in the hippodrome, and asked for a contribution from each. But soon he saw that he was accomplishing nothing and that his words were only empty talk. The majority deemed these burdensome and unwonted injunctions to be wholly intolerable and became clamorous and seditious. The emperor, blamed by some for squandering the public wealth (τὰ κοινὰ) and distributing the provinces to his kinsmen, all of whom were worthless and benighted, quickly discarded the proposal, as much as saying that it was not he who had introduced the scheme.

zh: • 1204年初，都城人民意识到阿莱克修斯四世（Alexios IV）只是拉丁人的傀儡。身为目击者与参与者的科尼亚特斯（Choniates）对事件的叙述值得长篇引录：
en: • In early 1204, the people of the City realized that Alexios IV was only a puppet of the Latins. The narrative of events from Choniates, who was an eyewitness and participant, deserves to be quoted at length:

zh: 都城的民众（τὸ δημῶδες τῆς πόλεως）表现得像大丈夫，敦促皇帝与士兵一同参加对敌〔即拉丁人〕的斗争，因为他们是爱国者（πατριώταις）……但伊萨克〔其父〕鼓励他无视粗鄙民众的闲言碎语，把最高荣誉授予那些使他重返本国的人〔拉丁人〕……一些与拉丁人为伍者把人民的审议当作老妇的闲话而不予理会，他们逃避与拉丁人作战，比一群鹿逃避咆哮的狮子还要快……都城民众找不到任何并肩作战、拔剑对抗拉丁人的盟友，便开始起来叛乱，像一把烧开的水壶喷出蒸汽那样，把怒骂一股脑发泄到两位皇帝身上……大批喧嚷的人群聚集在大教堂；元老院、主教会议与可敬的教士被迫在那里集会，共同商议谁应继任皇帝……单纯而善变的群众宣称，他们不再愿意受安格洛斯家族统治，除非先选出一位合他们心意的皇帝，否则集会不散。
en: The City’s populace (τὸ δημῶδες τῆς πόλεως), acquitting themselves like men, pressed the emperor to take part with the soldiers in the struggle against the enemy [i.e., the Latins], as they were patriots (πατριώταις)... But Isaakios [his father] encouraged him to ignore the idle talk of the vulgar populace and to bestow the highest honors on those who had restored him to his country [the Latins]... Some who associated with the Latins as comrades ignored the people’s deliberations as old wives’ gossip, being quicker to avoid battle with the Latins than an army of deer with a roaring lion... The City populace, finding no fellow combatant and ally to draw the sword against the Latins, began to rise up in rebellion and, like a boiling kettle, to blow off steam of abuse against the emperors... A great and tumultuous concourse of people gathered in the Great Church; the senate, the assembly of bishops, and the venerable clergy were compelled to convene there and deliberate together as to who should succeed as emperor... The multitude, simpleminded and volatile, asserted that they no longer wished to be ruled by the Angelos family, and that the assembly would not disband unless an emperor to their liking was first chosen.

zh: 前面的清单选取了这样一些事件：君士坦丁堡人民在宗教、政治、财政与王朝事务上主动捍卫并推行自己的观点，或当他们不喜欢某位皇帝、想要除掉他时。同样，我在这里只列了人民作用为主的事件；当我们转向人民作用为次但仍具决定性的叛乱时，我们就再也无法回避“舆论”的作用了——那是政治争端各方都试图密切监测、迎合与争取的东西。
en: The preceding list is a selection of episodes when the people of Constantinople took the initiative to defend and enforce their views when it came to religious, political, fiscal, and dynastic matters, or when they disliked an emperor and wanted to get rid of him. Again, I have listed here only episodes in which the role of the people was primary; when we turn to the rebellions in which their role was secondary but still decisive, we will then no longer be able to avoid the role of “public opinion,” that which all sides in political disputes were trying to monitor closely, cater to, and win over.

zh: 即便在这一小组事件中，我们也能辨识某些反复出现的行为模式。人民通常高呼关于罗曼尼亚或反对皇帝及其官员的口号，扰乱
的运作，并在赛马场集会。值得注意的是，“挖出他的骨头！”这一口号与对
（帝国执法与秩序维护的枢纽）的攻击，早在六世纪就有记载。我们在导致米海尔五世覆灭（1042年）的事件中两者都见到了。由于都城人民大概并不阅读前代的历史，这意味着他们有自己的传统——甚至是仪式，或许甚至是“制度”——用以发动民众起义，这些传统在许多世纪中保持相对稳定。我们将在下文再次遇到并讨论其中一些。
en: Even in this small set of episodes we can discern some recurring patterns of behavior. The people typically chant slogans about Romanía or against the emperor and his officials, they disrupt the operations of the
and they assemble in the hippodrome. It is noteworthy that the slogan “Dig up his bones!” and the attack on the

(the hub of imperial law-and-order enforcement) are attested as early as the sixth century. We saw both in the events that led to the fall of Michael V (in 1042). As the people of the City were presumably not reading histories of earlier eras, this means that they had their own traditions—rituals even, perhaps even “institutions”—for instigating a popular uprising, traditions that remained relatively stable over the course of many centuries. We will encounter and discuss some of these again below.

zh: 同样重要的是要注意，人民在所有他们关心的事务上都宣示自己的意志，世俗的与宗教的皆然。在下面的详细分析中，我将集中于前者，主要是内战与继承问题——人民在其中起了（且通常被要求起）决定性作用。但在宗教问题上他们并不被动，也不等着别人告诉他们怎么做。
在其关于民众参与宗教争议的里程碑式研究结尾，蒂姆·格雷戈里（Tim Gregory）试图解释皇帝为何竟然会理会舆论。他倾向于引用务实因素（尤其是他们想保住皇位的愿望），但当他必须解释最初是什么在“安抚人民”与“保住皇位”之间建立了因果联系时，他最终诉诸残存的“古罗马‘民主’传统的火花”，即“权力最终来自被统治者”的观念。
格雷戈里可以理解地不愿退回到这一点，因为这会使史家显得只讲观念而有些不切实际。于是有了那些限定词，如“火花”一词和“民主”周围的警示引号。但如果没有别的办法解释这一动力，我们就应当废除那些限定语及其背后的顾虑。那不是什么火花。正如本章其余部分将表明的，那是一场随时可能爆发、吞噬皇帝的燎原大火。
en: It is also important to note that the people asserted their will in all matters that interested them, secular as well as religious. In the following detailed analysis I will concentrate on the former, mostly on civil wars and the succession problem where the people played (and were typically asked to play) a decisive role. But they were not passive when it came to religious issues, and did not wait to be told what to do.

At the end of his landmark study of popular participation in religious controversies, Tim Gregory tries to explain why the emperors paid any attention to public opinion at all. He prefers to cite pragmatic factors (especially their desire to stay on the throne), but when he has to explain what created the causal link between appeasing the people and staying on the throne in the first place, he ultimately invokes the surviving “spark of the old Roman ‘democratic’ tradition,” the idea “that power came ultimately from the governed.”

Gregory is understandably reluctant to fall back on this, because it makes historians seem “idealistic” and a bit wooly headed. Hence the qualifiers, such as the word “spark” and the scare quotes around “democratic.” But if there is no other way to explain the dynamic, we should abolish the qualifiers and the bad conscience that comes with them. It was no spark. As the rest of this chapter will show, it was a conflagration that could erupt and consume emperors at any time.

zh: 舆论与权力争夺：一种内战理论
en: Public Opinion and Contests for Power: A Theory of Civil War

zh: 在我们对皇帝职位意识形态的理解（它奠基于绝对的神学原则）与拜占庭政治史混乱而不可预测的现实之间，始终存在张力。最令人不安的是：据称拜占庭人相信其皇帝由上帝任命统治，与他们反叛他的轻易和频繁之间的落差。所有皇帝都以某种方式宣称自己由上帝任命统治，但这种神恩并未保护他们免遭阴谋、叛乱与民众起义。当然，有可能某个想反叛的人因宗教顾虑而作罢，但史料中几乎没有这方面的证据（部分因为史料倾向于不记录未发生的事件）。叛乱者与合法皇帝之间的界限始终是可渗透的。拜占庭政治史通篇充斥着阴谋与密谋，导致“皇帝屡屡遭到暗杀，任何关于拜占庭绝对君权的政治理论，都必须因此有所保留”。
en: There has always been a tension between our understanding of the ideology of the imperial office, which is grounded in absolute theological principles, and the messy and unpredictable realities of Byzantine political history. What is most troubling is the gap between the alleged belief of the Byzantines that their emperor was appointed to rule by God and the ease and frequency with which they rebelled against him. All emperors asserted that they were appointed to rule by God in some way, but this divine favor did not protect them from plots, rebellions, and popular uprisings. It is of course possible that someone thinking of rebelling decided against it because of religious scruples, but there is little evidence of that in the sources (in part because sources tend not to record events that failed to happen). The boundary between rebels and legitimate emperors was always porous. Byzantine political history is marked throughout by plots and conspiracies leading to the “regular imperial assassinations that have to be seen as qualifying any absolutist political theory in Byzantium.”

zh: 当学者试图解释这一落差时，他们诉诸一种在抽象阐述拜占庭政治理论原则时否则从不使用的语言。格雷戈里在上引段落中使用了“罗马民主”。保罗·勒梅尔（Paul Lemerle）关于拜占庭叛乱者有这样一段话（再次注意警示引号与条件限定词的使用）：
en: When scholars try to account for this gap, they resort to language that they otherwise never use when setting forth the principles of Byzantine political theory in the abstract. Gregory made use of “Roman democracy,” in the passage quoted above. Paul Lemerle had this to say about Byzantine rebels (note, again, the use of scare quotes and conditional qualifiers):

zh: 篡位具有一种意义、几乎一种政治功能。它与其说是非法行为，不如说是正当化过程的第一步……在
与篡位者之间，相似之处多于对立之处。因此存在两种不同的正当性观念，一种是“王朝的”，另一种人们或可称之为（罗马意义上的）“共和的”。二者并不真正冲突，反而相互强化。
en: Usurpation had a significance and almost a function that was political. It was less an illegal act than the first act in the process of legitimation... Between the basileus and the usurper there is more parallelism than opposition. Hence the existence of two different notions of legitimacy, one “dynastic” and the other one might call (in the Roman sense) “republican.” These are not truly in conflict, but rather reinforce each other.

zh: 事实上，二者常常冲突，而那时哪个占主导就毫无悬念。在这种冲突的理想形态中，在位皇帝或叛乱者只有一种王朝“权利”（姑且这么说），而其对手背后站着“共和国”。这里谁会胜出毫无疑问。如我们所见，王朝主张并非一种权利，而只是皇帝（或潜在皇帝）可以提出的众多修辞论据之一。在现实世界中，唯有恰当的权力平衡才能使皇帝安全，而该等式中的关键因素之一就是我们的史料所称的舆论。我们在米海尔五世的案例中鲜明地看到了这一点。他覆灭的叙事是用“声望”的语言铸成的：佐伊如何拥有它，米海尔如何试图获得它，以及他如何失去它——连同他的皇位与双眼。
en: In fact, they often were in conflict, and there was then no question about which was dominant. In an ideal form of this conflict, the sitting emperor or rebel has only a dynastic “right,” such as it was, whereas his opponent has the “republic” behind him. There is no doubt who will prevail here. As we have seen, dynastic claims were not a right but only one among many rhetorical arguments that an emperor (or potential emperor) could make. In the real world, only the right balance of power could make an emperor safe, and one of the key factors in that equation was what our sources call public opinion. We saw this strikingly in the case of Michael V. The narrative of his downfall was cast in the language of “popularity”: how Zoe had it, how Michael tried to gain it, and how he lost it—along with his throne and eyes.

zh: 尽管关于拜占庭阴谋与叛乱的研究很多，却很少关注舆论在其中的作用。我指的不仅是社会与政治精英对帝国状况及在位皇帝功过的看法，还包括人口多数对这些事情的意见。这里首先指君士坦丁堡的人民，尽管本章后面将论证行省居民的重要性。这一遗漏部分源于史家把政治视为精英之间、或精英与皇帝之间的事务，而人民只是被动旁观者。让-克洛德·谢内（J.-C. Cheynet）关于963至1210年权力争夺的经典研究，完全把它们当作精英竞争的函数。他只用了三页谈人民，概述精英对他们的屈尊态度，而且似乎暗示人民缺乏集体认同。至于叛乱者为争取公众支持可能做过什么，他只有两小段谈谶语的传播。
然而在一处他引人入胜地提到“舆论的多变与皇权的脆弱”，
表述完美但未展开。这正是我们这里要接手的主题，以补充谢内那在其他方面颇为详尽的分析。
en: While we have many studies of plots and rebellions in Byzantium, little attention has been paid to the role in them of public opinion. By this I mean not only the opinion of the social and political elite regarding the state of the empire and the merits or flaws of the current emperor but the opinions of the majority of the population about such things. In the first instance, this would be the people of Constantinople, though a case will be made later in this chapter for the importance of the provincials as well. This omission is partly a result of the fact that historians consider politics as a business taking place among the elite, or between the elite and the emperor, with the people as passive bystanders. J.- C. Cheynet’s classic study of contests for power between 963 and 1210 casts them entirely as a function of elite competition. He devotes only three pages to the people, which summarize the elite’s condescending attitudes toward them, and he seems to suggest that the people lacked a collective identity. As for what rebels might have done to garner public support, he has two brief paragraphs on the dissemination of oracles.
Yet in one place he tantalizingly refers to “the versatility of public opinion and the fragility of imperial power,”
which is perfectly stated albeit undeveloped. That is the theme that we will take up here, to complement Cheynet’s otherwise thorough analysis.

zh: 现代分析遗漏舆论，部分源于某些理论家的假设：过去的文化按照与我们不可通约的规范与范畴运作，因此我们不应对它们使用据称“现代”的术语，如宗教、艺术、国家、主权、民族、舆论、无神论等等。保罗·韦纳（Paul Veyne）就罗马帝国（包括拜占庭）的舆论提出了一个极端论点：
en: The omission of public opinion from modern analyses stems in part from the assumption made by some theorists that past cultures operated according to norms and categories that were incommensurate with our own, and that we should therefore not use allegedly “modern” terms such as religion, art, the state, sovereignty, the nation, public opinion, atheism, and a host of others, in relation to them. Paul Veyne made an extreme case with regard to public opinion in the Roman empire (including Byzantium):

zh: 那时并不存在舆论现象，它无法与绝对权利长期共存，因而也无法与……一位是神或依神权统治的君主共存。因为舆论不在于反叛、默默忍受或不满，而在于
自己有权不满，且君主即便可能被其大臣误导，仍可能有过错……如今舆论对政府作出评判；那时，人民爱戴其君主，思想正确者则赞美服从乃每个忠顺臣民的本分……人们没有政治意见，政治讨论亦不为人知。
en: There did not then exist the phenomenon of public opinion, which cannot coexist for long with absolute right, or consequently with... a sovereign who is a god or who reigns by divine right. For public opinion does not consist in rebelling, suffering silently or being discontented, but in

that one has the right to be discontented and that the monarch, even when his ministers may have misled him, can nevertheless be at fault... Today public opinion passes judgment on the government; then, the people loved their sovereign and right-thinking persons praised submission as the duty of every loyal subject... People did not have political opinions and political discussion was unknown.

zh: 今天很少有人会同意这种极端表述，但仍没有人表明它在拜占庭的情形下究竟错得多么离谱，或通过研究拜占庭人在不顺从、也不大爱戴其统治者时的政治意见、讨论与
来驳斥它。
还有一种理论声称“舆论”只能产生在现代资产阶级社会。
在某些圈子里这是一条公理，
并很可能阻碍了进一步探究。当这些论点的倡导者并不第一手了解前现代社会的史料、且被奉为专属现代的概念又被恰恰定义成只适用于现代时，我对这类论证保持怀疑——于是通过反向工程产生了一种同义反复（例如，用民族可能借以产生的
即工业化来定义民族，而不是用它作为集体认同与组织形式的属性来定义）。一概而论的否定性论证在正面证据面前会崩溃，所以让我们考察那些证据。
en: Few today would agree with this extreme formulation, but still no one has shown just how wrong it is in the case of Byzantium or refuted it by studying the political opinions, discussions, and
of the Byzantines at the times when they were not being submissive or much in love with their ruler.
There is also a body of theory which claims that “public opinion” is a function of modern bourgeois society.
In some circles this is an axiom,

and has probably blocked further inquiry. I remain skeptical of such arguments when their proponents do not know the sources for premodern societies at first hand and when the concept that is being upheld as exclusively modern is also defined in precisely such a way as to apply only to modernity, thus, through reverse-engineering, producing a form of tautology (for example, by defining the nation through

by which it may emerge, industrialization, rather than by its properties as a form of collective identity and organization). Sweeping negative arguments collapse in the face of positive evidence, so let us consider that evidence.

zh: 我将从一个只配进历史脚注（如果配的话）的事件开始，但它有力地说明了当君士坦丁堡舆论
一场权力争夺时会发生什么。1056年，塞奥多拉去世、米海尔六世（Michael VI）即位之际，已故皇帝君士坦丁九世的表亲狄奥多西·莫诺马霍斯（Theodosios Monomachos）自认为有皇位主张，便召集依附者穿城游行，抗议政权并宣布自己竞选皇位。他前往
释放囚犯（如我们所见，这是一种仪式性行动），却发现宫殿已武装起来对付他。于是他前往圣索菲亚大教堂，希望得到牧首与民众的拥立，却发现那里也对他关闭。越多人得知正在发生什么，街道就越空。被所有人抛弃后，狄奥多西最终与儿子坐在教堂前，最终被流放佩尔加蒙（Pergamos）。
他严重误判了自己的声望。人民在这里的作用是通过不作为而具决定性的。狄奥多西指望他们介入。史家佐纳拉斯（Zonaras）补充说，“民众”后来为他编了首小调：“愚蠢的莫诺马霍斯，脑子里冒出什么就干什么。”
en: I will start with an episode that belongs in the footnotes of history (if that) but which powerfully illustrates what could happen when Constantinopolitan public opinion

in a political contest. In 1056, upon the death of Theodora and the accession of Michael VI, Theodosios Monomachos, a cousin of the late emperor Konstantinos IX who believed that he had a claim to the throne, gathered his dependents and processed through the City, protesting against the regime and declaring his candidacy for the throne. He went to the

and freed the prisoners (a ritual action, as we saw), but he found the palace armed against him. He then went to Hagia Sophia, hoping that the patriarch and the people would acclaim him, but he found that closed too. The more people found out what was happening, the emptier the streets became. Abandoned by all, Theodosios finally sat before the church with his son and was eventually exiled to Pergamos.

He had badly misjudged his popularity. The people’s role here was decisive through inaction. Theodosios was counting on them to get involved. The historian Zonaras adds that the “popular masses” later made up a ditty for him, “Stupid Monomachos, did whatever jumped into his head.”

zh: 狄奥多西以为会发生什么？至少他所希望的，是一场把他抬上皇位的民众起义。这并非不可能，但一切取决于在位政权多么不受欢迎、以及“人民”如何看待他个人。让我们看看其他政治人物在不受欢迎的政权下争取民众支持的事件，情形
有多么不同。
en: What did Theodosios think would happen? What he hoped for, at least, was a popular uprising that would lift him to the throne. It was not beyond the realm of possibility, but it all hinged on how unpopular the current regime was and how “the people” perceived him personally. Let us see how differently it
have gone by looking at other episodes when political figures made a bid for popular support against unpopular regimes.

zh: • 695年，将军莱昂提乌斯（Leontios）因在查士丁尼二世治下担心性命，前往

，释放并武装了囚犯。随后他与部下奔往君士坦丁广场，号召人民到圣索菲亚大教堂集会，并派传令官到都城各处宣布消息。人民集会时，牧首卡利尼科斯（Kallinikos）支持莱昂提乌斯，于是人民侮辱查士丁尼（ἐδυσφήμει）并高呼“挖出他的骨头！”——这是一种诅咒形式，标志着民众对某人权威的拒斥，此处即皇帝的权威（我们在579年与1042年也听到过）。人民涌向赛马场，次日查士丁尼被带出、被割去鼻子；他们要求处死他，但莱昂提乌斯饶了他。人民欢呼莱昂提乌斯为皇帝。
他显然知道舆论敌视查士丁尼，但奔往广场仍是巨大冒险。一切取决于事到临头人民会怎么做。事实上，即便在莱昂提乌斯被欢呼之后、“违背他的意愿”，人民仍围捕了查士丁尼的一些亲信，把他们拖到陶里广场烧死。
en: • In 695, the general Leontios, fearing for his life under Justinian II, went to the

where he released and armed the prisoners. He then ran to the forum of Constantine with his men calling on the people to assemble at Hagia Sophia and sending heralds to the different parts of the City to proclaim the news. When the people assembled, the patriarch Kallinikos supported Leontios, whereupon the people insulted Justinian (ἐδυσφήμει) and cried out, “Dig up his bones!” a form of curse that signaled popular rejection of someone’s authority, in this case the emperor’s (we heard it also in 579 and 1042). The people rushed to the hippodrome, and on the next day, Justinian was brought out and his nose was cut off; they demanded that he be killed, but Leontios spared him. The people acclaimed Leontios emperor.

He had apparently known that public opinion was hostile to Justinian, but he took a huge risk in running to the forum. All depended on what the people would do when matters came to a head. In fact, even after Leontios’s acclamation and “against his wishes,” the people still rounded up some of Justinian’s associates, dragged them to the forum Tauri, and burned them.

zh: • 1181年，新近去世的曼努埃尔一世·科穆宁（Manuel I Komnenos）之女玛丽亚公主，为了支持安德罗尼库斯·科穆宁（Andronikos Komnenos），策划反对廷臣阿莱克修斯·科穆宁（Alexios Komnenos，官居
）——后者与曼努埃尔的第二任妻子安条克的玛丽亚（Maria of Antioch）勾结，以控制幼帝阿莱克修斯二世（Alexios II）。她的图谋暴露后逃往圣索菲亚大教堂寻求庇护，但民众纷纷站出来支持她，尤其是赤贫者，她在他们中很受欢迎。当
威胁要把她逐出教堂时，她在入口设岗并加固教堂。很快，军队单位倒向她一边，开始诅咒
与皇后。他们在米利翁（Milion）与赛马场这样做，直到民众公开起义。这导致流血，并最终使
倒台、安德罗尼库斯·科穆宁崛起。
科尼亚特斯的叙述表明，“这不是一场自发的暴动，而是经过数日的宣传与组织人民才公开起义，尽管他们坚决敌视现政府。”
en: • In 1181, the princess Maria, daughter of the recently deceased Manuel I Komnenos, plotted on behalf of Andronikos Komnenos against the courtier Alexios Komnenos (a

in rank), who had taken up with Manuel’s second wife, Maria of Antioch, in order to control the child-emperor, Alexios II. Her designs exposed, she fled to Hagia Sophia seeking sanctuary, but the people rallied to her cause, especially the very poor, among whom she was popular. When the
threatened to evict her from the church, she placed guards at the entrance and fortified it. Soon, military units went over to her side and began to curse the
and the empress. They did this at the Milion and in the hippodrome until the populace rose up in open rebellion. This led to bloodshed and, eventually, the downfall of the
and the rise of Andronikos Komnenos.

Choniates’s narrative suggests that “this was not a spontaneous riot, but it took several days of propaganda and organization before the people rose in open revolt, even though they were solidly hostile to the current government.”

zh: • 1185年，伊萨克·安格洛斯（Isaakios Angelos）杀死了安德罗尼库斯一世·科穆宁（Andronikos I Komnenos）派来对付他的人、担心性命，便穿城逃往圣索菲亚大教堂，一路喊着自己所做的事并挥舞刀剑。人民成千上万涌出，决定保护他及其家人对抗安德罗尼库斯。到早晨，人民已决定伊萨克应统治、而现已不受欢迎的安德罗尼库斯应被废黜。
后者试图用一封短信（大概是宣读给他们听的）使人民恢复理智，但徒劳。人民欢呼伊萨克，从
释放囚犯，开始侮辱安德罗尼库斯，并围攻宫殿。安德罗尼库斯逃走，被俘，数日后被交给人群，人群把他撕成碎片。
我们的主要史料尼基塔斯·科尼亚特斯（Niketas Choniates）没有丝毫暗示这不是一场民众行动。他的叙事有一条不容置疑、甚至不言自明的公理：谁是皇帝，由人民说了算；而我们上面已看到科尼亚特斯对1203–1204年事件的看法，证明了同一点。
en: • In 1185, having killed the man whom Andronikos I Komnenos had sent against him and fearing for his life, Isaakios Angelos fled through the City to Hagia Sophia, shouting out what he had done and waving his sword. The people turned out in the thousands and decided to protect him and his family against Andronikos. By morning, the people had decided that Isaakios should rule and that Andronikos, who was now unpopular, should be dethroned.
The latter tried to bring the people to their senses with a brief letter that was presumably read out to them, but to no avail. The people acclaimed Isaakios, freed the prisoners from the
began to insult Andronikos, and besieged the palace. Andronikos fled, was captured, and days later was turned over to the crowd, who tore him to pieces.

There is no hint in our main source, Niketas Choniates, that this was anything but a popular action. It is an unquestioned and even unspoken axiom of his narrative that the emperor is who the people say he is, and we saw above Choniates’s view of the events of 1203–1204, which proved the same.

zh: 狄奥多西·莫诺马霍斯在1056年所希望的就是那种民众支持，或许不那么血腥。他试图激发一场自发的欢呼。莱昂提乌斯这样的将军与贵族（如莫诺马霍斯家族与安格洛斯家族）可能属于精英，但在其政治生涯最关键的时刻，他们必须冒险一搏，把身家性命押在自己对民意的判断上。他们无法保证除自己的依附者外是否会有人出来支持。有时并没有，如下面这些案例。
en: Theodosios Monomachos was hoping for that kind of popular support in 1056, if perhaps less bloody. He was trying to stimulate a spontaneous acclamation. Generals such as Leontios and aristocrats (such as the Monomachoi and Angeloi) may have belonged to the elite, but at the most crucial moment of their political career they had to take a leap of faith and bet everything on their assessment of popular opinion. They could not guarantee whether anyone other than their own dependents would turn out in support. Sometimes they did not, as in the following cases.

zh: • 阿莱克修斯·科穆宁在即位前，曾于1078年代表被废的米海尔七世（Michael VII）的兄弟或儿子君士坦提乌斯·杜卡斯（Konstantios Doukas）尝试夺位。他把紫色凉鞋穿在君士坦提乌斯脚上，让他以公开仪仗穿城前往宫殿。“但
异口同声地高喊，他们不愿受他统治。”君士坦提乌斯恳求阿莱克修斯别再帮他。
阿莱克修斯随后未能说服宫中的尼基弗鲁斯三世·博塔内亚特斯（Nikephoros III Botaneiates）承认君士坦提乌斯为继承人。
en: • Alexios Komnenos, before he became emperor, once made a bid on behalf of Konstantios Doukas, the brother or son of the deposed Michael VII, in 1078. He placed the purple sandals on Konstantios’s feet and processed him through the City to the palace. “But the
with one voice, loudly shouted that they did not want to be ruled by him.” Konstantios begged Alexios to stop helping him.
Alexios then failed to persuade Nikephoros III Botaneiates in the palace to recognize Konstantios as his heir.

zh: • 1185年伊萨克·安格洛斯成功后（见上文事件），其前任之子伊萨克·科穆宁（Isaakios Komnenos）在圣索菲亚大教堂尝试同样策略，但失败了。
en: • After the success of Isaakios Angelos in 1185 (see the episode above), his predecessor’s son, Isaakios Komnenos, tried the same tactic in Hagia Sophia but failed.

zh: 在这种情况下，人们无法轻易强迫舆论。正如人民可以大量涌出终结一个王朝（695、1042、1185年），当一个王朝受欢迎且他们感到它受威胁时，他们也会团结起来保卫它。
en: One could not easily force public opinion under such circumstances. Just as the people could turn out in numbers to end a dynasty (in 695, 1042, and 1185), so too could they rally to defend it when it was popular and they perceived it as being under threat.

zh: • 642–643年，将军瓦伦提诺斯（Valentinos）试图从君士坦斯二世手中夺取皇权，可能是试图说服元老院欢呼他，“但君士坦丁堡人民听闻后便起来反对他，他立刻脱下了〔皇〕袍。”经谈判后，他被任命统率军队。
但644–645年，凭借他在都城的3000士兵，他再次尝试夺位。归于塞贝奥斯（Sebeos）名下的编年史记载，当他的一名部下殴打牧首时，人群被激怒，扑向他。他们强行拽着他的脚把他拖到都城中心，用火把他烧死。瓦伦提诺斯得知后，浑身颤抖。人群立刻扑向他，把他从屋里拖出斩首……他们确认君士坦斯继续坐在王位上。
en: • In 642–643, the general Valentinos sought to seize the imperial power from Konstas II, possibly by trying to persuade the senate to acclaim him, “but when the people of Constantinople heard, they arose against him, and straightaway he put off the [imperial] robes.” After a negotiation, he was placed in command of the armies.

But in 644–645, with 3,000 soldiers that he had in the City, he made another attempt on the throne. The chronicle attributed to Sebeos reports that when one of his men struck the patriarch, the crowd was aroused, and they fell on him. They forcibly dragged him by the foot into the middle of the City and burned him with fire. Valentinos was informed, and trembling gripped him. Immediately the crowd descended on him, and dragging him out of his house cut off his head... They confirmed Konstas on the throne of the kingdom.

zh: • 944年，病中的罗曼努斯一世·拉卡佩努斯（Romanos I Lakapenos）被其子斯特凡诺斯（Stephanos）与君士坦丁逮捕并流放。但当消息传出，马其顿王朝继承人君士坦丁七世（Konstantinos VII）的地位乃至性命正受威胁（他被罗曼努斯一世边缘化二十余年，但未受伤害），“全体人民”聚集到宫门要求见他，于是拉卡佩努斯家族只得让他在民众面前露面，恢复他的地位。不久后他把他们打包打发去与父亲一同流放。
无人反对。
en: • In 944, a sick Romanos I Lakapenos was arrested and exiled by his sons Stephanos and Konstantinos. But when word got out that the position and even the life of the heir of the Macedonian dynasty, Konstantinos VII, were being threatened (he had been sidelined by Romanos I for over twenty years, but not harmed), “the entire people” gathered at the palace gates and demanded to see him, whereupon the Lakapenoi had to display him and restore him to his position. Soon afterward he sent them packing to join their father in exile.
No one objected.

zh: 我们迄今考察的事件都发生在都城内，人民在那里享有压倒性的人数优势。这些事件可视为某种选举——诚然是不规则的——但人民有机会作出选择，而他们作出的选择决定了事态的结局。我们仍未发现任何案例，其中我们的史料或任何当事方认为人民的干预是不正当的、违反
政治规范的。我们也很少发现人民干预对解决问题不具决定性的案例。拜占庭的政治史，是一部被革命性民众干预所打断的君主制史。
en: We have so far considered events that took place within the City where the people enjoyed a crushing numerical advantage. These events can be seen as elections of a sort, irregular ones to be sure, but the people had the opportunity to make a choice and they did so with decisive consequences. We have still not found any case where our source, or any of the parties involved, considered the people’s intervention to be illegitimate, in violation of the political norms of the

And we have also found few cases where the people’s intervention was not decisive in settling the issue. The political history of Byzantium was that of a monarchy punctuated by revolutionary popular interventions.

zh: 迄今呈现的事件都发生在都城内。然而，当一支叛军逼近都城时会发生什么？在这种时候，人民往往不是权力斗争的被动旁观者。在其他研究领域，指出内战属于政治史是多余的，但拜占庭学家却可能完全从宗教角度看待它们，视之为关于谁获上帝恩宠的神学争论。
但那个问题是事后才解决的。战争进行时，谁拥有
支持的问题更为紧迫。
en: The episodes presented so far took place within the City. What happened, however, when a rebel army approached the City? At such times the people were often not passive spectators of the struggle for power. In other fields of research it would be redundant to point out that civil wars count as political history, yet Byzantinists are capable of seeing them exclusively in religious terms, as being theological disputes over who had God’s favor.
But that question was settled afterward. While the war was raging, the question of who had the
on his side was more pressing.

zh: • 我们史料中关于斯拉夫人托马斯（Thomas the Slav）叛乱及其围攻君士坦丁堡（821–823年）的叙事主轴，是叛乱者与其对手米海尔二世（Michael II）的相对声望。在叙述叛乱起源时，《塞奥法尼斯续编》（Theophanes Continuatus）强调，托马斯相信米海尔二世因据传与异端团体有关联、其说话方式与低劣道德而为所有人憎恨（ὑπὸ πάντων μισούμενος）；相比之下，托马斯认为自己会因更讨人喜欢的个性（及其他原因）而受欢迎得多。“他以为都城人民一看到他在那里，就会出于对米海尔的憎恨而为他敞开城门。但他这一希望落空了；事实上他甚至遭到侮辱与嘲笑，”于是他诉诸武力，最终徒劳。
托马斯可能错了，但这段文字表明了拜占庭叛乱者的思维过程。他们简直只差为竞逐皇位召集焦点小组做民意测试，或者成立“筹备委员会”了。
en: • The narrative axis in our sources for the rebellion of Thomas the Slav and his siege of Constantinople (821–823) is the relative popularity of the rebel versus that of his opponent, Michael II. In recounting the origin of the rebellion, Theophanes Continuatus emphasizes that Thomas believed that Michael II was universally hated (ὑπὸ πάντων μισούμενος) because of his rumored affiliation with a heretical group, his manner of speech, and low moral qualities; by contrast, Thomas thought that he himself would be far more popular because of his more agreeable personality (among other reasons). “He thought that the people of the City would throw open the gates for him as soon as they saw him there, simply out of their hatred for Michael. But he failed in this hope; in fact, he was even insulted and covered in ridicule,” at which point he resorted to arms, to no avail in the end.

Thomas may have been wrong, but this passage is indicative of the thought-process of the Byzantine rebels. They were but a step away from having focus-group testing or “exploratory committees” for their bid for the throne.

zh: • 963年，当尼基弗鲁斯·福卡斯（Nikephoros Phokas）进军都城要求被欢呼为皇帝时，都城最有权势者、代表年幼的巴西尔二世（Basileios II）与君士坦丁八世（Konstantinos VIII）执政的约瑟夫·布林加斯（Ioseph Bringas）发现自己处境危险，“因为他因难以接近而绝不为市民所爱……他完全无能在逆境中讨好并左右舆论。本需要用温和讨好的言辞来抚平人群的态度，而他却倾向于刺激和激怒他们。”他给了两名部下士兵，他们试图平息都城日益增长的骚乱，“但人民被激怒并诉诸武力，在近战中抵抗他们，迫使他们落荒而逃。”他的政敌、
（内侍长）巴西尔（Basileios）开始对布林加斯的文职支持者使用暴力，都城陷入混乱。巴西尔还安排部分舰队倒向尼基弗鲁斯，“经人民与元老院同意”，尽管具体如何达成不清楚。“与此同时……在主干道、集市与后街，人们欢呼征服者尼基弗鲁斯。”布林加斯随后投降，“全城居民”在尼基弗鲁斯抵达时迎接了他。
《仪典之书》（
）中保存的记述（可能出于巴西尔的授意）赋予人民在解决冲突、偏向福卡斯方面更突出的作用。
en: • In 963, when Nikephoros Phokas was marching on the capital demanding to be acclaimed as emperor, the most powerful man in the capital, Ioseph Bringas, ruling on behalf of the young Basileios II and Konstantinos VIII, found himself in a dangerous position “because he was by no means beloved of the citizens on account of being so unapproachable... He was totally incapable of flattering and swaying public opinion in adverse circumstances. It would have been necessary to massage the crowd’s attitude with soft and flattering speeches, while he tended rather to prickle and aggravate them.” He gave soldiers to two of his men and they tried to put down the growing turmoil in the capital, “but the people became enraged and resorted to force, and resisted them in close combat, and forced them into open flight.” His political enemy, Basileios the

(imperial chamberlain), began to use violence against Bringas’s civilian supporters, and the City descended into mayhem. Basileios also arranged for part of the fleet to go over to Nikephoros, “with the approval of the people and the Senate,” though how exactly this was secured is unclear. “While this was going on... in the main thoroughfares, the marketplaces, and the back streets they were acclaiming Nikephoros the conqueror.” Bringas then surrendered and “the entire city population” received Nikephoros upon his arrival.
The account preserved in the
(probably at Basileios’s instigation) gives the people an even more prominent role in settling the conflict in Phokas’s favor.

zh: • 1047年利奥·托尔尼克斯（Leon Tornikes）的军队逼近时，“都城中的众多人群”不确定病中的君士坦丁九世是否还活着、或是否应出城加入叛军。这迫使皇帝反复出面与他们相处。
托尔尼克斯的希望是“都城人民会因皇帝未按他们认为应有的方式对待他们而对他愤怒。”
当他在城墙前列阵时，他的部下开始提醒站在城墙上的人在君士坦丁治下所受的苦难，并承诺只要他们打开城门就能摆脱它。届时他们将拥有一位“宽厚而有用的皇帝，他会怜悯地对待他们，并以打击蛮族的战事和由此获得的战功壮大罗马的力量。”
这是及时的政治修辞——拜占庭版的公共关系、一场竞选演说——因为皇帝恰在那一年不顾许多主张鹰派政策者的反对，把佩切涅格（Pecheneg）部落安置在多瑙河罗马一侧。
也正逢其时都城守军空虚，意味着这场公关努力的对象是被征召守城的市民。目击者普塞洛斯（Psellos）指出，这些临时士兵并不中用，“全城都在考虑倒向叛军。”
遭受军事失败后，君士坦丁“把注意力转向都城民众，试图赢回他们的欢心。”托尔尼克斯同样也让他的俘虏恳求同一“人群”开恩并谴责皇帝的恶行。
尽管有军事背景，这里进行的是一场争夺舆论的政治斗争，皇帝最终靠耗尽叛军耐心而获胜。
en: • When the armies of Leon Tornikes approached in 1047, “multitudes in the City” were unsure about whether the ailing Konstantinos IX was still alive or whether they should go out and join the rebel. This forced the emperor to come out repeatedly and spend time with them.
Tornikes’s hope was that “the people of the City would be angry with the emperor as he did not treat them the way they thought he should.”

When he drew up his battle line before the walls, his men began to remind those who were standing on them of the evil they had endured under Konstantinos and promised that they would be free of it if only they opened the gates. They would then have a “lenient and useful emperor, who would treat them compassionately and augment the Roman power with wars and trophies against the barbarians.”

This was timely political rhetoric—the Byzantine version of public relations, a stump speech—for the emperor had just that year settled Pecheneg tribes on the Roman side of the Danube against the objections of many who advocated a hawkish policy.

It also happened at that time that the City was denuded of a garrison, which meant that this public relations effort was being addressed to the citizens who had been drafted for the defense. Psellos, a witness, notes that these makeshift soldiers were no good and that “the entire City was thinking of going over to the rebel.”

After suffering a military defeat, Konstantinos “turned his attention to the populace of the City and tried to win back their favor.” Tornikes likewise had his prisoners implore the same “multitude” for mercy and condemn the evil deeds of the emperor.
Despite the military context, what was going on here was a political struggle over public opinion, which the emperor ultimately won by waiting out the patience of the rebel’s forces.

zh: • 让我们也考察1057年米海尔六世的军队被叛军伊萨克·科穆宁击败后随之而来的斗争中对舆论的争夺——或更确切地说，各方如何援引舆论来使自己的行动正当化。米海尔六世起初想逃，但被谋士劝阻：“也许若能确保市民支持他就能活命，于是他试图向他们喊话，用礼物与赏赐争取他们。”
他通过使者同意立伊萨克为共治者，但借口“我害怕
的群众与元老院阶层，因我不确定他们会否批准此计划”而请求推迟该行动。
事实上他极不受欢迎。他自己的使者回到现已逼近都城的伊萨克那里，向他保证“全城群众都站在他一边；他只需逼近都城，他们就会驱逐老头，以凯旋之歌与颂诗迎接
米海尔随后试图“用礼物、金钱、过分的荣誉及一切能讨好并巧妙争取人民、确保其支持与忠诚的东西，来加固市民对自己的支持。”
但人民与元老院无论如何都开始反对他，人群聚集到圣索菲亚大教堂。普塞洛斯长篇描述他们如何涵盖每个社会阶级、职业、年龄与性别。
最终牧首凯鲁拉里奥斯（Keroularios）宣布米海尔六世被废，命他退位，“因为这就是群众的要求。”
牧首用这番话掩盖了自己的密谋，但他选择这样的措辞，充分说明了拜占庭政体的意识形态基础。最终，“米海尔是在被市民殴打与震动之后，才终于不情愿地退出皇位的。”
en: • Let us also consider the battle for public opinion—or rather, how it was invoked by all sides to legitimate their actions—in the struggle that ensued after the armies of Michael VI were defeated by the rebel Isaakios Komnenos in 1057. Michael VI first thought of flight but was restrained by his counselors: “Maybe he would survive if he could secure the support of the citizens, so he tried to address them and to win them over with gifts and bounties.”
Acting through envoys, he agreed to make Isaakios his partner but asked to postpone that action on the pretext that “I am afraid of the multitude of the
and the senatorial order, as I am not certain that they will approve the plan.”

In fact, he was highly unpopular. His own envoys went back to Isaakios, who was now much closer to the City, and assured him “that the entire urban multitude was on his side; that he need only approach the City and they would expel the old man, receiving
with triumphal songs and hymns.”
Michael then tried to “reinforce the citizens’ support for himself with gifts, money, excessive honors and whatever else flatters and artfully wins over a people, securing their support and loyalty.”

But both people and senate began to turn against him anyway, and the multitudes gathered in Hagia Sophia. Psellos goes on at length about how they included every social class, profession, age, and sex.
Finally, the patriarch Keroularios declared Michael VI deposed and commanded him to step down “because this was what the multitude were demanding.”

The patriarch was hiding his own plot behind these words, but it speaks volumes about the ideological basis of the Byzantine polity that he would phrase it that way. In the end, “it was only after being bruised and shaken by the citizens that Michael did eventually reluctantly withdraw from the throne.”

zh: • 1078年尼基弗鲁斯·布里恩尼奥斯（Nikephoros Bryennios）叛乱时，他“相信〔君士坦丁堡〕市民对皇帝〔米海尔七世〕与
（总务长官）〔尼基弗里齐斯（Nikephoritzes）〕愤怒且深恶痛绝（δι᾽ ὀργῆς καὶ μίσους），当其兄弟〔约安尼斯（Ioannes）〕率列阵大军抵达时他们会倒向他一边，并会在与他达成协议后接他入城。”这名叛将的兄弟试了与三十年前利奥·托尔尼克斯相似的修辞策略，但失败了，尤其当其部下焚毁一处郊区、使民众疏远时。
后来布里恩尼奥斯被带到更成功的对手尼基弗鲁斯三世·博塔内亚特斯面前，后者回顾这一刻，斥责他不被人民认为配（ἄξιος）得上皇位、并因他们的侮辱而蒙羞，
仿佛他在谈论一场声望竞赛（而他自己赢了）。
en: • When Nikephoros Bryennios rebelled in 1078, he “trusted that the citizens [of Constantinople] were furious with and deeply hated (δι᾽ ὀργῆς καὶ μίσους) the emperor [Michael VII] and the

[Nikephoritzes] and would go over to his side when his brother [Ioannes] arrived at the head of a large army in formation, and that they would receive him into the City having come to an agreement with him.” The rebel’s brother tried similar rhetorical tactics to those of Leon Tornikes thirty years earlier, but failed, especially when his men set a suburb on fire, which alienated the populace.

When Bryennios was later brought before his more successful rival Nikephoros III Botaneiates, the latter reflected back on this moment and castigated him for not being deemed worthy (ἄξιος) of the throne by the people and being dishonored by their insults,
as if he were talking about a popularity contest (which he himself had won).

zh: • 关于米海尔七世，阿塔莱亚特斯（Attaleiates）说，到1078年“舆论（κοινὴ γλώσσα）对他的无知与肆意的傲慢不满，并认为他应对从四面八方涌来的灾祸负责。”
处于这种境地的皇帝很少能长久。如今，阿塔莱亚特斯《历史》（

）的最后一节基本是对米海尔的敌人与继任者博塔内亚特斯的颂辞，我们不应把其中一切照单全收。即便如此，它仍有力证明了一次成功的篡位如何在事后被铸为人民的选择（这并不是说它事实上不也是人民的选择），正如博塔内亚特斯把布里恩尼奥斯的失败呈现为人民的选择（见上一事件）。阿塔莱亚特斯告诉我们，当米海尔七世与全体元老院在布拉赫奈宫时，圣索菲亚大教堂的人民开始欢呼极受欢迎的博塔内亚特斯。“他们抛却对皇帝的一切恐惧，行事仿佛自己是一个民主政体（δημοκρατία）。”
争夺舆论之战再次打响，正如我们见过的其他案例。米海尔七世与另一位叛将布里恩尼奥斯如今都送去自己的宣言宣读给人民，但后者以侮辱回应，因为他们想要博塔内亚特斯：“人民的意志与势头与他同在。”
叛军在君士坦丁堡受到的接待，正值大规模拥戴他的民众示威之中。
en: • Regarding Michael VII, Attaleiates says that by 1078 “public opinion (κοινὴ γλώσσα) was displeased with his ignorance and unbridled arrogance and believed that he was at fault for the evils that were pouring in from all sides.”
An emperor in such a position rarely lasted for long. Now, the final section of the

of Attaleiates is basically a panegyric for Michael’s enemy and successor Botaneiates and we should not take everything in it at face value. Even so it offers strong evidence for the way in which a successful usurpation could be cast after the fact as the people’s choice (which is not to say that it was not that in fact, too), just as Botaneiates had presented the failure of Bryennios as the people’s choice (see the previous episode). Attaleiates tells us that when Michael VII was at the Blachernai palace with the entire senate, the people in Hagia Sophia began to acclaim Botaneiates, who was superpopular. “They cast off all fear of the emperor and conducted themselves as if they were a democracy (δημοκρατία).”

The battle for public opinion was on again, just as in the other cases we have seen. Both Michael VII and the alternative rebel Bryennios now sent their proclamations to be read to the people, but the latter responded with insults because they wanted Botaneiates: “the will and momentum of the people were with him.”
The rebel’s reception in Constantinople occurred in the midst of massive popular demonstrations in his favor.

zh: 我在本章迄今讨论的证据多来自十一世纪。一些史家得出结论：这一时期君士坦丁堡人民的权力源于偶然、暂时的因素，不适用于拜占庭历史的其余部分，

而帝国政治的动态确有波动，尤其在这个两个王朝、两种治理模式（马其顿与科穆宁）之间动荡的过渡期。但有压倒性的理由反对“十一世纪政治属于与拜占庭历史其余部分不同范畴”的观点。首先，该世纪的史料恰好比其他时期更丰富。对其他时期我们依赖简短条目或更关注统治者个人美德或恶行而非公共领域运作的史料。其次，我们看到人民在六至七世纪、十二至十三世纪初也展现自己的政治力量，其方式揭示出与十一世纪相同的形式与底层假设，例如“挖出他的骨头！”的呼喊与从
释放囚犯。
“挖出某人的骨头”基本意味着“打倒某人”。
这一语境中另一个“技术”术语是
（“不配！”）的呼喊，人民借此收回对某位皇帝的恩宠。这个贯穿我们整个时期的术语，是人民在皇帝欢呼时高呼的
（“配！”）的反面与撤销。
在五世纪末至十三世纪之间，这里存在深层的结构与象征连续性。没有充分理由相信十一世纪是反常的，除了它记录更详。
en: Much of the evidence I have discussed so far in this chapter comes from the eleventh century. Some historians have concluded that the power of the people of Constantinople in this period resulted from contingent and temporary factors that do not apply to the rest of Byzantine history,

and certainly there were fluctuations in the dynamics of imperial politics, especially in this turbulent period of transition between two dynasties and two modes of governance (the Macedonian and the Komnenian). But there are overwhelming objections to the view that eleventh-century politics belong to a different category from the rest of Byzantine history. First of all, the sources for that century happen to be fuller than for other periods. For the others we rely on brief entries or sources that are more interested in the personal virtues or vices of the rulers than the workings of the public sphere. Second, we have seen the people flex their political muscles also in the sixth to seventh century and in the twelfth to early thirteenth century in ways that reveal the same forms and underlying assumptions as the eleventh, for example, the cry “Dig up his bones!” and the freeing of prisoners from the
“Dig up the bones of x” basically meant “Down with x.”
Another “technical” term in this context was the cry of
(“Unworthy!”), by which the people withdrew their favor from a particular emperor. This term, which was used throughout our period, was the inverse and cancelation of
which the people chanted at an emperor’s acclamation.

There are deep structural and symbolic continuities here between the late fifth and thirteenth centuries. There is no good reason to believe the eleventh was aberrant, except in that it is better documented.

zh: 斯拉夫人托马斯相信舆论能决定此类争夺，把我们带到820年代；而似乎同样的动态也支配着513–515年维塔利安（Vitalianos）三次进军城墙（反对阿纳斯塔修斯）。我们关于维塔利安叛乱的史料贫乏，
但其策略似乎旨在确保民众支持以图夺取都城。那么，这就是政治领域的一个基本结构特征，早在公元500年就已开始。正如1203–1204年事件所揭示，即便科穆宁王朝改变了治理方式，这种政治机制也延续了下来。它并非某些人所称的“边缘”现象。
en: Thomas the Slav’s belief in the efficacy of public opinion to decide such contests takes us to the 820s, and it seems that the same dynamic governed the three marches up to the walls by Vitalianos in 513–515 (against Anastasios). The sources that we have for Vitalianos’s rebellion are meager,

but his strategy seems to have aimed at securing popular support in an effort to take the City. That, then, was a basic structural feature of the political sphere, starting already in 500 AD. As the events of 1203–1204 reveal, it even survived the Komnenian revolution in governance. It was not a “marginal” phenomenon, as some have called it.

zh: 因此我们可以重新考察记录较差时期发生的事件，以及叛军兵临城下时民众的政治。
en: We may therefore reconsider events that occurred in the more poorly documented periods and the politics of the populace when a rebel army was before the gates.

zh: • 705年查士丁尼二世在保加尔人支持下从流放地返回重夺皇位。尼基弗鲁斯（Nikephoros）说，“他在布拉赫奈城墙边扎营三天，要求都城居民（τοὺς τῆς πόλεως）接他为皇帝；但他们以恶毒的侮辱打发他。然而他夜间带少数人爬进都城输水道，以此方式夺取了君士坦丁堡。”
遗憾的是，我们无法重建城墙上谈判的性质或当事方，也不大了解当时的舆论（佐纳拉斯后来润色了其史料，使场景更生动）。
查士丁尼如何从显然敌对的民众手中重夺都城？在此我们必须记住，所有这些都是从一个敌视查士丁尼、试图使他显得不正当的原始史料转述而来的。
塞奥法尼斯（Theophanes）有相同叙事，但补充说查士丁尼是以熟悉的“挖出他的骨头！”呼喊赢得都城的。
这团结了人民去推翻皇帝提比略三世·阿普西马尔（Tiberios III Apsimar）。但为何这次他们加入查士丁尼？
en: • In 705 Justinian II returned from exile to reclaim his throne with Bulgar support. Nikephoros says that “for three days he encamped by the walls of Blachernai and demanded that the inhabitants of the City (τοὺς τῆς πόλεως) receive him as emperor; but they dismissed him with foul insults. However, he crept with a few men at night into the aqueduct of the City and in this way captured Constantinople.”

Unfortunately, we cannot reconstruct the nature or the parties to the negotiations that took place on the walls, nor do we know much about public opinion at that time (Zonaras later embellished his sources and made the scene more graphic).

How did Justinian retake the City from an apparently hostile populace? At this point we must remember that all this is being reported secondhand from an original source that was hostile to Justinian and trying to make him seem illegitimate.
Theophanes has the same narrative but adds that Justinian won the City with the familiar shout of “Dig up his bones!”
This rallied the people to take down the emperor Tiberios III Apsimar. But why did they join Justinian this time?

zh: • 717年，即被迫退位两年后，阿纳斯塔修斯二世（Anastasios II）在保加尔人支持下试图重夺君士坦丁堡。据塞奥法尼斯，他进军君士坦丁堡但“都城不接受他”，他被交出。
据尼基弗鲁斯，他致信一些关键人物，希望他们为他打开都城，但密谋败露了；他集结军队但未及都城，只到赫拉克利亚（Herakleia）。皇帝利奥三世（Leon III）向保加尔人许诺，他们便交出了他。
佐纳拉斯又有更富戏剧性、更重民众作用的叙事：阿纳斯塔修斯“以为自己会被民众接受。但人民不愿接受他。”
有可能十二世纪中叶写作的佐纳拉斯是以十一世纪更熟悉的模板来塑造他对这些事件的版本，但他这样做未必全错。
en: • In 717, two years after his forced abdication, Anastasios II tried, with Bulgar support, to regain Constantinople. According to Theophanes, he marched on Constantinople but “the City did not accept him” and he was surrendered.

According to Nikephoros, he wrote letters to some key players, hoping that they would open the City for him, but they were betrayed; he gathered his army but did not make it quite as far as the City, only to Herakleia. The emperor, Leon III, made promises to the Bulgars, and they surrendered him.
Zonaras, again, has a more dramatic and more populist narrative: Anastasios “thought that he would be accepted by the populace. But the people would not accept him.”

It is possible that Zonaras, writing in the mid-twelfth century, was modeling his version of these events on the more familiar template of the eleventh century, but he may not have been entirely wrong to do so.

zh: 二十年前琳达·加兰（Lynda Garland）从她对民众权力的考察（聚焦十一、十二世纪，但我认为普遍适用）得出以下结论。

根据我们史料中的形象，都城人民无处不在（除宫殿内），并准备评论各类事件。他们对时事消息灵通，对统治者的行为既怀疑又明察，而他们自己的行动往往出于一种正义感。他们一直留心有没有机会介入都城政治，能在数小时内动员。他们倾向于作为一个群体行动，很少分裂到对立两边；少数群体很少成功。人民觉得自己有权选择皇帝，似乎并不害怕皇帝或帝国政府。对他们的裁决无法上诉。“因此，皇帝无论多么强大或专制，都必须持续保持对民众情绪的觉察……并确保安抚人民……就国家重大事件咨询他们或告知他们。”政策事实上被调整以迎合舆论，我们已反复看到。
en: Twenty years ago Lynda Garland drew the following conclusions from her survey of popular power (focusing on the eleventh and twelfth centuries though, I believe, applicable generally).

According to the image in our sources, the people of the City were present everywhere, except in the palace, and were ready to comment on all types of events. They were well informed about current events, and cynical and discerning about the actions of their rulers, while their own actions were often informed by a sense of justice. They were on the alert for opportunities to intervene in the politics of the City and could mobilize within hours. They tended to act as one group and were rarely split on opposite sides; minority groups were rarely successful. The people felt that they had the right to choose emperors and did not seem to be afraid of the emperor or the imperial government. It was impossible to appeal their verdict. “As a result, emperors, however powerful or autocratic, continually had to maintain an awareness of popular feeling... and ensure that they propitiated the people... and consulted them or informed them about events of national importance.” Policies were in fact adjusted to cater to public opinion, which we have seen repeatedly.

zh: 在打断拜占庭政治生活的权力争夺中，现代学术倾注全部注意力的精英们充分意识到民众干预可能起的关键作用，并处处表现出接受那些干预的正当性。毕竟，“以另一方的名义行使权力，总是冒着权力在名义上所属的一方，可能要把实权连同其形式一并收回。”
这正是我们在一个君主制共和国中所预期的。
的理论与政治的实践相对应。
en: In the contests for power that punctuated Byzantine political life, the elites on which modern scholarship has lavished all its attention were fully aware of the crucial role that popular interventions could play, and gave every sign of accepting the legitimacy of those interventions. After all, “to exercise power in the name of another party is always to run the risk that the formal titleholder will attempt to reclaim its substance as well as its form.”
This is exactly what we would expect in a monarchical republic. The theory of the
corresponded to the practice of politics.

zh: 因此我提出一种关于拜占庭内战的新理论。折磨帝国的众多内战并不代表其政治框架的失败、甚至未必代表其弱点。它们只代表在位皇帝未能维持控制、尤其是未能维持自身声望的失败。战争处于挑战在位皇帝权威的光谱的一端。它们给帝国人口、尤其是都城人口，提供了在两个（或更多）候选人之间的选择。直白地说，内战与其他挑战是一种选举形式。“争夺”是罗曼尼亚政治的核心，因为谁能执掌权力，要由共和国各方共同判断、共同认可，无人享有绝对的掌权资格，而他们的容许也只是暂时的。那么，“内战”就是帝国对共和国选举的回答：相互竞争的潜在领袖争夺民众的恩宠。它是帝国管理其政治的一种方式。这种对拜占庭内战的解释说明了以下醒目事实：历史上没有任何国家有过更多“对政体结构或意识形态毫无改变”的内战。拜占庭内战通常只关乎人事。让我们不要忘记，旧共和国最后一个世纪的政治本身就包含相当剂量的周期性内战与城市暴力，并最终走向“帝国”的共和式君主制（事实上，我们对晚期共和国了解如此之多，正是因为拜占庭人着迷于罗马内战，保存了关于那一时期的许多记录）。
en: I therefore propose a new theory of civil war in Byzantium. The many civil wars that wracked the empire did not represent a failure or necessarily even a weakness of its political framework. They represented only failures on the part of sitting emperors to maintain control and, chiefly, their own popularity. Wars were at one extreme of a spectrum of challenges to a sitting emperor’s authority. They gave the population of the empire, and especially of the capital, a choice between two (or more) candidates. To be blunt, civil wars and other challenges were a form of election. “Contestation” was at the heart of politics in Romanía, because there was no absolute right to hold power beyond what the elements of the republic in their collective judgment would allow, and their sufferance was always temporary. “Civil war,” then, was the empire’s answer to the elections of the Republic: rival potential leaders competing for the favor of the populace. It was one way by which the empire managed its politics. This interpretation of Byzantine civil war explains the following striking fact: no state in history ever had more civil wars that changed nothing about the structure or the ideology of the polity. Byzantine civil wars were usually only about personnel. Let us not forget that the politics of the old Republic in its final century had themselves included a hefty dose of periodic civil war and urban violence, which culminated in the republican monarchy of the “Empire” (in fact, we know so much about the late Republic because the Byzantines, fascinated by Roman civil war, preserved many records about that very period).

zh: 那么，除军事层面外，内战本质上是争夺舆论的政治竞争，取决于对受欢迎与不受欢迎的感知。多数在几个月内结束。尽管造成破坏，它们也确保拜占庭由总体上有能力、受欢迎的统治者统治。一切的核心是“舆论”，即全体人民对其统治者的看法。与韦纳的断言相反，人们确有政治意见，政治讨论似乎盛行，舆论无时无刻不在评判政府。但这对我们理解拜占庭政治领域的意涵仍有待阐发。我相信这无法在一部专著、更不用说几页内完成，但可以作一些初步观察。
en: Above and beyond their military aspects, then, civil wars were essentially political contests over public opinion and hinged on perceptions of popularity and unpopularity. Most were over within a few months. Despite the damage that they did, they also ensured that Byzantium was ruled by generally capable and popular rulers. At the heart of it all lay “public opinion,” or what all the people believed about their rulers. Contrary to what Veyne asserted, people did have political opinions, political discussion seems to have been rampant, and public opinion passed judgment on the government, all the time. But the implications of this for our understanding of the Byzantine political sphere have yet to be worked out. That cannot be done, I believe, in one monograph, much less in a few pages, but some preliminary observations can be made.

zh: 声望的政治
en: The Politics of Popularity

zh: 根据迄今呈现的证据，一种熟悉的拜占庭政治领域模型已不再站得住脚。那是一个遵循颂辞惯例、把皇帝视为政治领域本质的模型。所有人都服从他超验的权威，“政治”只发生在精英的小圈子里。在这个模型中人民是旁观者，没有制度可供追求其政治利益。“帝国对都城‘群氓’的态度限于提供慈善、善举与公共节日的货币发放……民众扮演重要但被动的仪式角色。”
偶尔他们确实暴动，但那是暴力、孤立的事件，没有意识形态意义。
en: According to the evidence presented so far, a familiar model of the Byzantine political sphere is no longer tenable. That is a model which, following the conventions of panegyric, regards the emperor as the essence of the political sphere. All were subject to his transcendent authority and “politics” happened only within the tiny circles of the elite. In this model the people were spectators, with no institutions through which to pursue their political interests. “Imperial attitudes toward the ‘mob’ of the City were limited to the provision of charity and good works and monetary distributions on public festivals... the populace played an important, if passive, ceremonial role.”
On occasion, they did riot, but these were violent, isolated incidents with no ideological significance.

zh: 这个模型必须被替换，而非修补。没有人民同意就没有皇帝正当性。唯有它授权皇帝以罗马人民的名义、作为“罗马人的皇帝”（而非“罗马皇帝”，那是现代术语）统治。此外，人民同意可随时收回，直到作出让步或出现更可接受的对手。一切取决于皇帝相对潜在对手在臣民中的受欢迎程度。在拜占庭反叛在很大程度上意味着评估那种平衡。唯有在一个以民众拥戴为根基的政治文化中，一个人才能仅凭声望就觊觎皇位或被他人视为可行竞争者。拉克坦提乌斯（Lactantius）想象伽列里乌斯（Galerius）与戴克里先（Diocletian）如何打算处理君士坦丁（Constantine，当时尚未掌权，却已是潜在对手）的声望所带来的问题。
查士丁尼的廷臣惧怕贝利撒留（Belisarios）的声望。
据称米海尔四世（Michael IV）惧怕米海尔·凯鲁拉里奥斯（Michael Keroularios，在其成为牧首前）的声望。
曼努埃尔一世（Manuel I）把阿克苏赫（Axouch）送进修道院，因为他同样惧怕其声望。
声望只有在共和式君主制中才能成为如此量级的政治问题。正因如此，比皇帝更受欢迎是危险的，但它也煽动野心。
en: This model must be replaced, not just tweaked. There was no imperial legitimacy without popular consent. Only that authorized an emperor to govern in the name of the Roman people as “the emperor of the Romans” (not as “the Roman emperor,” which is a modern term). Moreover, popular consent could be retracted at any time until concessions were made or a more acceptable rival emerged. All depended on how popular the emperor was with his subjects in relation to potential rivals. Rebelling in Byzantium in large part meant assessing that balance. Only in a political culture whose foundations were populist could a man aspire to the throne or be considered a viable competitor by others, simply on the basis of his popularity. Lactantius imagined how Galerius and Diocletian planned to handle the problem posed by the popularity of Constantine (then still a private citizen, but a potential rival).
Justinian’s courtiers were terrified of the popularity of Belisarios.
Michael IV allegedly feared the popularity of Michael Keroularios (before he became patriarch).
Manuel I sent Axouch to a monastery because he too feared his popularity.
Popularity can become a political problem of this magnitude only in a republican monarchy. For that reason it was risky to be more popular than the emperor, but it also fueled ambitions.

zh: 这对社会的政治化（至少在都城）有戏剧性后果（下文也将论证行省社会）。帝国政治中没有绝对稳定的点。皇权随时可被收回并重新分配，有时很快，这意味着所有臣民都在不断评估自己的选项，决定是否喜欢皇帝并把他与当时其他显要人物作比较。皇帝方面则处于永久试用期、因而焦虑与不安的状态中治理与生活。他们必须随时维持声望。拜占庭政治史就是他们做得如何的故事。潜在篡位者总在评估自己相对在位皇帝的声望。
en: This has dramatic consequences for the politicization of society, at least in the capital (though a case will be made below for provincial society too). There was no point of absolute stability in imperial politics. Imperial authority could always be recalled and reassigned, sometimes quickly, which meant that all subjects were constantly assessing their options, deciding whether they liked the emperor and comparing him to other leading men of the day. Emperors, for their part, governed and lived in a state of permanent probation, and hence of anxiety and insecurity. They had to maintain their popularity at all times. The history of Byzantine politics is the story of how well they did this. Potential usurpers were always assessing their own relative popularity compared to that of the sitting emperor.

zh: 我们迫切需要关于拜占庭舆论的聚焦研究，材料是充足的。据我所知，只有一部专著哪怕间接涉及该主题，即尼克-卡特琳·库特拉库（Nike-Catherine Koutrakou）一部被引甚少的法文博士论文。
在不讨论叛乱动态或其意识形态意涵的情况下，库特拉库展示了皇帝多么在意赢得并保持舆论站在自己一边：“确保舆论的认可是帝国政府持续的关切。”
她考察了受欢迎与不受欢迎的词汇，以及我们史料指称公众的术语。虽然难以推断皇帝为左右舆论而向其宣传的具体受众，但关键的是“在拜占庭心态中，公众始终是非人格的。”

试图使它既人格化又限于精英的是现代史家。相比之下，拜占庭政治家想象自己的行动正被遍及整个罗马社会的公众，不因个人身份或社会分层而分别看待密切注视与评估。让我举一个醒目例子。尼基塔斯·科尼亚特斯记载，当阿莱克修斯一世·科穆宁（Alexios I Komnenos）垂死、被妻子施压要把他们的儿子约安尼斯（Ioannes）排除出继承时，他回应说若那样做他将成为 τὸ Πανρώμαιον（全罗马社会）的笑柄。这就是罗马人民那个非人格的集体，所有成功皇帝都对其意见敏感。
en: We urgently need focused studies of Byzantine public opinion, for which there is ample material. To my knowledge, there is only one monograph that even tangentially touches on the topic, a little-cited dissertation in French by Nike-Catherine Koutrakou.

Without discussing the dynamics of rebellion or its ideological implications, Koutrakou shows how concerned emperors were to gain and keep public opinion on their side: “to assure the approbation of public opinion was a constant preoccupation of the imperial government.”

She surveys the vocabulary of popularity and unpopularity, and the terms by which our sources refer to the public. While it is difficult to make inferences about the specific audiences to which emperors addressed their propaganda in order to sway public opinion, it is crucial that “the public, in the Byzantine mentality, remained impersonal.”

It is modern historians who have tried to make it both personal and limited to the elite. Byzantine politicians, by contrast, imagined that their actions were being closely watched and evaluated by an undifferentiated, impersonal, and national audience. Let me give one striking example. Niketas Choniates reports that when Alexios I Komnenos was dying and was being pressured by his wife to exclude their son Ioannes from the succession, he responded by saying that if he did that he would become a laughingstock to τὸ Πανρώμαιον, the entirety of Roman society. This is the impersonal collectivity of the Roman people to whose opinion all successful emperors were sensitive.

zh: 我们需要研究在拜占庭什么品质使人得到拥戴或遭到厌弃，以及人们在何种场合留意和议论这些品质。史料常提到这位或那位皇帝“试图赢得臣民的好感。”

这是如何做到的？在此我们必须小心，不要因所见不显得特别深刻就鄙视我们的研究对象。为摆正视角，让我们不要忘记现代选民似乎偏好一个政治家胜过另一个的理由。带着这一点，我们不应鄙视拜占庭公关体系空洞的道德说教。所谓“君主之镜”（Mirrors of Princes）所敦促的品质，可能恰恰是那些提升皇帝在臣民中形象的品质。我们已看到其中一部作者阿加佩托斯（Agapetos）如何发出含蓄威胁：“臣民甘愿接受你的统治，你才能自认为统治稳固。因为不情愿的臣民一有机会就反叛。但被善意纽带所统治者，对其统治者的服从是坚定的。”
该传统中一部较晚文本指出“臣民是其统治者行为的严厉法官。”
那么这些文本可被视为生存手册，至少在舆论领域。582年提比略二世擢升莫里斯（Maurikios）登位时，指示他在臣民中培育善意而非恐惧，并欢迎批评。
他的史家塞奥菲拉克托斯（Theophylaktos）把这段话放在叙事开头，鉴于莫里斯在叙事结尾602年的遭遇，是严峻的反讽。在给皇后伊琳娜（Eirene）的信中，斯图狄奥斯的狄奥多罗斯（Theodoros the Stoudite）赞美她的良政、财政政策、宗教品质与博爱，并指出她由此“为自己保全王国的完整，你的臣民自愿同意你的统治。”
这次又是反讽，但非有意：伊琳娜被其首席财政大臣废黜（802年）。
en: We need studies of what qualities made a man popular or unpopular in Byzantium and in which contexts those qualities were perceived and discussed. Historical sources often mention that this or that emperor “tried to win over the good opinion of his subjects.”

How was this done? We must be careful here not to despise our subjects if what we see does not strike us as especially profound. To put matters in perspective, let us not forget the reasons for which modern voters seem to prefer one politician over another. With that in mind, we should not disdain the vapid moralizing of the Byzantine public-relations system. The qualities urged by the so-called Mirrors of Princes may have been precisely those that enhanced an emperor’s image among his subjects. We have seen how the author of one of them, Agapetos, delivers a veiled threat: “Consider yourself to rule safely when you rule willing subjects. For the unwilling subject rebels when he has the opportunity. But he who is ruled by the bonds of goodwill is firm in his obedience to his ruler.”
A later text in that tradition notes that “subjects are severe judges of their ruler’s actions.”

These texts, then, can be seen as survival manuals, at least in the field of public opinion. When Tiberios II raised Maurikios to the throne in 582, he instructed him to foster goodwill in his subjects, not fear, and to welcome criticism.

It was grimly ironic of his historian, Theophylaktos, to place this passage at the beginning of his narrative, given what happened to Maurikios at its end, in 602. In a letter to the empress Eirene, Theodoros the Stoudite praises her good measures, fiscal policies, religious qualities, and philanthropy, and notes that she thereby “preserves the integrity of the kingdom for yourself and your subjects willingly consent to your rule.”
More irony this time, but unintended: Eirene was deposed by her chief finance minister (in 802).

zh: 皇帝试图赢得舆论，既为总体也为具体政策。
臣民的忠诚不能视为理所当然。拜占庭人倾向于批评其统治者。有些案例我们看到皇帝设法“挽回局面”，因为他们在某件事上失了人心，已给自己带来麻烦。这往往意味着向舆论屈服。文职皇帝君士坦丁十世·杜卡斯（Konstantinos X Doukas）甚至被迫出都城不远行军，因为“
都公开辱骂他因吝啬而不出去对抗蛮族。”
他的回应可能使他显得软弱或工于算计——这是共和国中每个政治家（古代、中世纪或现代）的两难：他是出于恐惧做他认为人民想要他做的事，还是做他认为正确的事？朋友与敌人看法不同，这正是政治的素材。我们这里离“不受法律或舆论约束的绝对统治者”模型很远。
en: Emperors tried to win over public opinion generally but also for specific policies.

Subjects’ loyalty could not be taken for granted. The Byzantines were predisposed to be critical of their rulers. There are cases when we see emperors engaged in “damage-control,” as their unpopularity in some area became a liability. Often this entailed caving to public opinion. Konstantinos X Doukas, a civilian emperor, was even forced to march out of the capital a short distance because “
was openly reviling him for not marching out against the barbarians due to his stinginess.”

His response may have made him look weak or calculating—the dilemma of every politician, ancient, medieval, or modern, in a republic: is he doing what he thinks people want him to out of fear or what he thinks is right? Friends would see matters differently than enemies, the stuff of politics. We are far here from the model of the “absolute ruler unconstrained by either law or public opinion.”

zh: 考虑利奥五世（Leon V，813–820）。塞奥法尼斯的续编者（一个基本敌对的史料）说，他的美德实际是他想讨好
、可耻地购买臣民恩宠的产物，即迎合舆论。
同一史料承认狄奥菲洛斯（Theophilos，829–842）至少在理论上被认为是一位热诚维护正义的人，尽管作者认为他只是假装如此以防范任何反对他的叛乱。
当然，有比一个只是假装正义的皇帝更糟的事。有趣的是，至少据这些冷嘲的观察者的看法，共和国的道德语境能使一些皇帝比他们否则会成为的样子更体面。
en: Consider Leon V (813–820). The continuer of Theophanes, a mostly hostile source, says that his virtues were actually the product of his desire to fawn upon the
and to shamefully purchase his subjects’ favor, that is, to cater to public opinion.

The same source admits of Theophilos (829–842) that he was believed, at least in theory, to be a fiery lover of justice, though the author believes that he only pretended to be that in order to counter any rebellion against him.

There are worse things, of course, than an emperor who is only pretending to be just. It is interesting to see that, at least according to these cynical observers, the moral context of the republic could make some emperors more decent than they would otherwise have been.

zh: 拜占庭舆论现象可从许多角度考察。这里我看一个，即不受欢迎可能成为死刑判决；我选它是为了凸显所有皇帝与政治家所面临挑战的致命紧迫性，对照我们因过度依赖“帝国理念”而构建的更自满的治理模型。阴谋、叛乱与篡位——总之所有暴力政权更迭——通常以负面舆论为由正当化。我们不必接受这些记述每一条的历史可靠性（有些是事后写的），但一个持续的模式表明了拜占庭人如何思考、谈论并彼此教育及其统治者关于帝国政治。例如君士坦斯二世被谋杀（668年于西西里），因为他被君士坦丁堡人民憎恨（ἐμισήθη）。
我们已看到最被憎恨的查士丁尼二世、米海尔五世与安德罗尼库斯一世的遭遇。这些关于声望之力能促成政权更迭的主张，即便缺乏一种能解释它们的皇帝地位理论，也进入了我们的现代叙事。
于是史家在实践中把共和国视为理所当然，却不在理论上承认它。
en: There are many angles from which the phenomenon of public opinion in Byzantium can be examined. Here I will look at one, namely, that unpopularity could become a death sentence, and I choose this in order to highlight the lethal urgency of the challenge faced by all emperors and politicians in contrast to the more complacent model of governance that we have constructed by relying too much on the “imperial idea.” Conspiracies, rebellions, and usurpations—in sum, all violent regime-change—were commonly justified by reference to negative public opinion. We do not need to accept the historical reliability of every single one of these accounts, some of which were written after the fact, but a persistent pattern indicates how Byzantines thought, talked, and educated each other and their rulers about imperial politics. Konstas II, for example, was murdered (in Sicily, in 668) because he was hated (ἐμισήθη) by the people of Constantinople.

We have already seen what happened to the most hated Justinian II, Michael V, and Andronikos I. These claims about the power of popularity to effect regime-change pass into our modern narratives even in the absence of a theory of the imperial position that would explain them.
Thus historians take the republic for granted in practice without acknowledging it in theory.

zh: 803年，许多人加入巴尔达内斯（Bardanes）反对尼基弗鲁斯一世（Nikephoros I）的叛乱，因为税赋使他们憎恨（ἐμίσει）他。
尼基弗鲁斯二世·福卡斯（Nikephoros II Phokas）也变得“为所有人憎恨”，
这无疑便利了民众接受对他的谋杀。1059年伊萨克·科穆宁在一场不流血政变中被去职：普塞洛斯告诉我们他同样“被都城人民与相当一部分军队厌恶（ἀπεχθάνεται）”，佐纳拉斯说他被人民、元老院与军队憎恨（μισητός）。
1061年，君士坦丁十世·杜卡斯欣慰地发现他刚躲过的阴谋“只源于少数人；发动攻击的不是普遍共识与运动。这使他精神重振。”
如我们所见，米海尔七世面临许多叛乱，多得无法讨论。只需说舆论——阿塔莱亚特斯的 κοινὴ γλώσσα——“对他的无知与肆意的傲慢不满，并认为他应对从四面八方涌来的灾祸负责。”
任何政权在这种条件下都无法长存，他的也没有。相反，声望能把人推上顶峰：“对君士坦丁堡人民而言，〔安德罗尼库斯·科穆宁〕是地上的神，仅次于天上的那一位……他把整个都城拉到自己一边……几乎转眼间高低贵贱与中间阶层都赶去投靠他……他凭民众的力量登上最高权力。”
他当时的对手，即阿莱克修斯二世的摄政团，因废黜了一位受欢迎的牧首狄奥多西（Theodosios）而“被憎恨”。
又一个历史反讽，鉴于安德罗尼库斯的结局（在赛马场被撕碎）。
en: In 803, many joined the rebellion of Bardanes against Nikephoros I because they hated (ἐμίσει) him on account of the taxes.
Nikephoros II Phokas also became “hated by all,”

which certainly facilitated popular acceptance of his murder.
