Isaakios Komnenos was removed from power in 1059 in a bloodless coup: Psellos tells us that he too “was detested (ἀπεχθάνεται) by the people of the City and not a small part of the army,” Zonaras that he was hated (μισητός) by the people, senate, and army.

In 1061, Konstantinos X Doukas was relieved to discover that the plot he had just survived originated “in a few people only; it was not a universal consensus and movement that had launched the attack. This revived his spirits.”

Michael VII, as we saw, faced many rebellions, more than we can discuss. Suffice it to say that public opinion, Attaleiates’s κοινὴ γλώσσα, “was displeased with his ignorance and unbridled arrogance and believed that he was at fault for the evils that were pouring in from all sides.”

No regime could survive for long under such conditions, and neither did his. Conversely, popularity could propel one to the very top: “To the people of Constantinople [Andronikos Komnenos] was a god on earth, second only to the one in heaven... He brought the entire City over to his side... in almost no time those of high and low estate and those in between were all sailing to join him... He rose to supreme power through the strength of the populace.”
His opponents at that time, namely, the regency of Alexios II, were “hated” for having deposed a popular patriarch, Theodosios.
Another historical irony, given how Andronikos ended up (in pieces, in the hippodrome).

zh: 我们需要一项关于拜占庭“憎恨”作为政治术语的研究。考虑867年巴西尔一世（Basileios I）谋杀米海尔三世（Michael III）所给的理由。谋杀本身当然有多种动机，野心居首，但注意巴西尔的崛起如何在事后很久、在偏向他的史料中被呈现。米海尔刚收养巴西尔，就：
en: We need a study of Byzantine “hatred,” as a political term. Consider the reasons given for the murder of Michael III by Basileios I in 867. The murder itself had a number of motives, of course, ambition being at the top of the list, but note how Basileios’s rise was presented, long after the fact, in sources favorable to him. Michael had just adopted Basileios when he:

zh: 开始被元老院与
、被几乎所有身居行政职位与掌管公共事务者、也被军队与都城全体民众辱骂与嘘斥；皇帝通过一些亲信得知这些……发现自己不仅对公共事务疏忽，而且懒惰、完全不胜任、愚蠢，并害怕群众起义或反叛（ἐπανάστασιν ἢ ἀπόστασιν παρὰ τοῦ πλήθους），于是决定让另一人与自己共同处理政务并分享权力。
en: began to be reviled and booed by the Senate and the

and by almost all who were in positions of the administration and in charge of public affairs; and also by the armies and the entire populace of the City. The emperor learned these things through some associates... Discovering not only his own negligence with regard to public matters but also his laziness, total lack of suitability, and foolishness, and fearing an uprising or rebellion on the part of the multitude (ἐπανάστασιν ἢ ἀπόστασιν παρὰ τοῦ πλήθους), he decided to take on a partner in the management of public affairs and power.

zh: 换言之，巴西尔的崛起对应于、事实上就是民意的表达。文本明确说他的擢升是“依照在职者、全体民众、军队与将军、及帝国所有土地与城市中所有臣属群众的意愿。”
这当然是
（全民共识）的意识形态，此处偏向巴西尔、敌视米海尔。它实际上是民众欢呼仪式投射到政治史上。当米海尔的行径越来越坏时，巴西尔试图劝他抛弃恶行：“因为我们被憎恨（μισούμεθα），”他说，“被整个都城与元老院憎恨，侍奉上帝的主教们视我们为受诅咒之人，人人都在说我们的坏话、侮辱我们。”
我们应由此推断巴西尔别无选择只能杀他。要么如此，要么在一场普遍起义中与他一同被毁灭。这就是奉巴西尔之孙君士坦丁七世之命颁布的传记的逻辑，旨在粉饰他的生涯。辩护律师会主张“是舆论让他这么做的。”
en: In other words, the rise of Basileios corresponded to, in fact was the expression of, popular will. The text is explicit that his elevation was “according to the wish of those in office and the entire populace and the armies and generals and all the multitudes who were subject to the empire in all lands and cities.”
This was, of course, the ideology of

here in favor of Basileios and hostile to Michael. It was effectively the ceremony of popular acclamation projected onto political history. When Michael worsened, Basileios tried to persuade him to set aside his evil ways: “for we are hated (μισούμεθα),” he said, “by the entire City and Senate, the bishops of God regard as accursed, and everyone is saying terrible things about us and insulting us.”

We are meant to infer from this that Basileios had no choice but to kill him. It was that or be destroyed with him in a general uprising. Such was the logic of the biography issued at the command of Basileios’s grandson, Konstantinos VII, which was meant to whitewash his career. A defense lawyer would argue that “public opinion made him do it.”

zh: 被视为不受欢迎是危险的，对皇帝与职官皆然。当皇帝政策不受欢迎、他不得不把一些高官牺牲给人群时，下属往往得顶罪。相反，声望是公共服务生涯的首要资格——除非它令皇帝担忧。普塞洛斯强调自己作为魅力人物的品质如何便利了他在宫廷的崛起，也给我们留下了关于“政治型”人物最详细的讨论，他主要指皇帝的左右手而非皇帝本人。
普塞洛斯把讨好他人（事实上是形形色色的支持群体）的能力擢升为治国术的首要品质。例如他赞美前首相、后为牧首的君士坦丁·莱胡德斯（Konstantinos Leichoudes）能适应不同环境，从而既被军队也被政治阶层爱戴。
他甚至把古罗马国王图卢斯·霍斯提利乌斯（Tullus Hostilius）塑造成一个
（平民派）：“他从一开始就极受人民欢迎（δημοτικώτατος），并使所有公民成为他的朋友，”
接续更尚武的罗慕路斯（Romulus）与虔诚的努马（Numa）（普塞洛斯写这些肖像是作为米海尔七世的教学模范）。甚至被西西里的威廉二世（William II of Sicily）庇护的傀儡阿莱克修斯·科穆宁也“夸口整个罗迈斯〔=罗曼尼亚〕站在他一边、真心爱他”，希望凭诺曼武力在君士坦丁堡称帝。
仿佛他想的是一场声望竞赛，而非军事入侵。我们再次注意到他心中是一个无差别的、全国性的罗马受众。
en: It was perilous to be regarded as unpopular, for emperors as well as for magistrates. Subordinates often had to take the fall when an emperor’s policies became unpopular and he had to sacrifice some leading officials to the crowd. Conversely, popularity was a leading qualification for a career in public service—unless it worried an emperor. Psellos, who stressed how his own qualities as a charmer facilitated his rise at the court, has also left us with the most detailed discussions of the “political type” of man, by which he meant mostly the emperor’s right-hand man rather than the emperor himself.

Psellos elevates the ability to ingratiate oneself with others, in fact with a diverse and manifold constituency, to a leading quality of statecraft. For instance, he praises the ex– prime minister and later patriarch Konstantinos Leichoudes for being able to adapt himself to different circumstances so that he was beloved by both the army and the political class.
He even cast the ancient Roman king Tullus Hostilius as a
“He was very popular with the people (δημοτικώτατος) from the very beginning and made all of the citizens his friends,”

following the more martial Romulus and pious Numa (Psellos was writing these portraits as pedagogical models for Michael VII). Even the puppet Alexios Komnenos, harbored by William II of Sicily, “boasted that the entirety of Romaïs [= Romanía] was on his side and truly loved him,” hoping to become emperor in Constantinople by the strength of Norman arms.
It was as if he were thinking of a popularity contest, not a military invasion. We note again that he has an undifferentiated, national Roman audience in mind.

zh: 统治者与潜在篡位者都注视臣民、监测自己的声望，以评估保住或夺取皇位的机会。这使“人民”、“整个
”、“都城民众”或“罗曼尼亚”成为共和国政治的核心要素，或许甚至是其重心。史料给我们留下人民无处不在之感，他们“除宫殿内，似乎总在都城见证并评论各类重大时事。”
我们需要把这一要素纳入对拜占庭政治的理解。正如苏珊·雷诺兹（Susan Reynolds）就西方所论，“我们需要比惯常更多地关注普通人的政治观念。中世纪政治思想通常只或主要通过系统而学院化的作者著作来研究…… 然而政治思想并非政治哲学家、法学家或神学家的专利。”
en: Both rulers and potential usurpers looked to their subjects and monitored their popularity to assess their chances of staying on, or gaining, the throne. This made “the people,” “the entire

” “the populace of the City,” or “Romanía,” a central element of the politics of the republic, perhaps even its center of gravity. The historical sources leave us with a sense of the ubiquity of the people, who, “except for within the palace, always seem to be present in the City to witness and comment on significant current events of every sort.”

We need to factor this element into our understanding of Byzantine politics. As Susan Reynolds has argued regarding the West, “we need to pay more attention than we customarily do to lay political ideas. Medieval political thought is generally studied only, or largely, through the works of systematic and academic writers... Political thought is not, however, the prerogative of political philosophers, jurists, or theologians.”

zh: 部分挑战在于我们仍缺乏对拜占庭民众文化的恰当研究。
我指的不是民俗（它往往服务于民族主义议程），而更像一部《拜占庭人民史》（
）。我们已反复看到，人民并非只因除欢呼皇帝外没有正式制度疏导其能动性就无权无势。然而“人民”在很大程度上被从我们的历史中抹去，那些历史聚焦正式制度与“官方意识形态”，把民众干预铸为“群氓暴动”的反常事例。拜占庭人民如同罗马
（平民），“不是某种
（流氓无产阶级），而是一个拥有古老传统的阶级。”
杰里·托纳（Jerry Toner）的《古罗马的民众文化》（
）与我就拜占庭（其罗马的直接继承者与延续）所论共鸣。他说“非精英有强烈的社会正义感，它作为……一种‘道德经济’运作，以确保精英履行其对人民的社会义务……古罗马的民众文化不仅关乎民俗；它关乎人们如何有时嘲弄、颠覆与侮辱其上级；如何操纵精英以遂己愿；以及如何看穿权贵用以支配他们的意识形态。”
正是人民自己强制执行共和国的平民主义意识形态，即便在皇帝治下。在这种时刻皇帝先前宣示的共和原则，反过来成了评判他们的标准。“一旦理想确立，每个皇帝都可被对照它评判。而知道理想皇帝的属性为何，给了普通罗马人一种思考现实落差程度的方式。”
“石刑是民众正义的极致。”
社会上级（包括皇帝）被辱骂、成为民众机智的目标，而他们泰然处之被视为得体。
en: Part of the challenge is that we still lack a proper study of Byzantine popular culture.
I do not mean folklore, which has tended to serve nationalist agendas, but something more like a

We have seen repeatedly that the people were not powerless just because there were no formal institutions to channel their agency other than their acclamation of the emperor. Yet “the people” have been largely written out of our histories, which focus on formal institutions and “official ideologies” and cast popular interventions as aberrant instances of “mob riots.” The people of Byzantium, like the Roman
were “not some
but a class possessed of an ancient tradition.”
Jerry Toner’s

resonates with what I have argued about Byzantium, the direct heir and continuation of his Rome. He says that “the non-elite had a strong sense of social justice that operated as... a ‘moral economy’ to ensure that the elite fulfilled their social obligations to the people... Popular culture in ancient Rome was not just about folklore; it was about how people sometimes mocked, subverted and insulted their superiors; how they manipulated the elite to get something of their own way; and how they saw through the ideologies by which the powerful sought to dominate them.”

It was the people themselves who enforced the populist ideology of the republic, even under the emperors. At such moments the republican proclamations of the emperors came home to roost. “Once an ideal had been established, every emperor could be judged against it. And knowing what the attributes of an ideal emperor were gave ordinary Romans a way of thinking about the degree to which the reality fell short.”
“Stonings served as the ultimate in popular justice.”
Social superiors, including the emperors, were abused and made the targets of popular wit, and it was considered good form for them to take it in stride.

zh: 托纳呈现了一种充满活力的舆论文化与激烈的政治讨论。
其他史家试图揭示古罗马民众动员的威胁性动态，精英作者则试图贬低它。
很可能有足够证据让我们在比这里描述的宏观层面更细的层面理解拜占庭的这类群体。但即便在那一层面，我也主张民众文化的这一面在拜占庭比在帝国早期与晚期古代更强。这将颠倒那个熟悉（且陈旧）的元叙事：据它拜占庭朝加强专制与独裁的方向迈了一步。拜占庭可能比其前身元首制（Principate）与多米那特制（Dominate）更共和。
en: Toner presents a vigorous culture of public opinion and intense political discussion.
Other historians have tried to uncover the threatening dynamics of popular mobilization in ancient Rome, which elite authors sought to demean.

There might well be enough evidence for us to understand such groups in more detail in Byzantium, below the macro level at which they have been described here. But even at that level, I would propose that this aspect of popular culture was stronger in Byzantium than it had been in the early imperial period and late antiquity. This would reverse the familiar (and worn) metanarrative according to which Byzantium took a step in the direction of increased autocracy and despotism. Byzantium was probably more republican than its predecessors, the Principate and the Dominate.

zh: 贯穿我们整个时期，君士坦丁堡人民（可能行省亦然）经常嘲弄皇帝，或上演恶毒的戏仿滑稽剧，或唱侮辱性小调与歌曲，常带性内容。其中一些存世，更多在史学史料中被提及。莫里斯（582–602）正走向覆灭时，人民上演节目嘲弄他、唱关于他性生活与压制性政权的诗句。我们还有针对福卡斯（Phokas，602–610）、君士坦丁五世（Konstantinos V，741–775）、约安尼斯一世·齐米斯克斯（Ioannes I Tzimiskes，969–976）与狄奥法诺（Theophano，一个极有创意的性戏仿）的辱骂诗句、阿莱克修斯一世·科穆宁（1081–1118）等，此外史书中还提到骚乱期间也这样做。
有人甚至训练一只鹦鹉侮辱皇后欧芙罗叙涅（Euphrosyne）：“你这妓女，付个公道价！”
这就是皇帝必须耐心忍受的，此外还有一系列绰号，多不讨好：粗颈、背教者、屠夫、
（两眼瞳色不同）、大胡子、割鼻者、粪名、可萨人、口吃者、酒鬼、智者、生于紫室者、美少年、捻缝工、老头、减价票（
）。有些在位期间就在用。拜占庭人除了经常不忠，还拥有最不敬的帝国文化之一。
en: Throughout our period the people of Constantinople (and probably of the provinces too) regularly mocked emperors either by staging vicious parodic skits or by singing insulting ditties and songs, often with a sexual content. A number of them survive, and more are alluded to in historiographical sources. Maurikios (582–602) was heading to his downfall when the people staged shows to mock him and sang verses about his sexual life and repressive regime. We have also abusive verses addressed to Phokas (602–610), Konstantinos V (741–775), Ioannes I Tzimiskes (969–976), and Theophano (a highly inventive sexual parody), Alexios I Komnenos (1081–1118), and others, in addition to references in the histories that this was done during disturbances.
Someone even trained a parrot to insult the empress Euphrosyne, “You whore, pay a fair price!”
This is what emperors had to bear patiently, in addition to a range of nicknames, most of which were not flattering: Thick Neck, Apostate, Butcher,
(eyes of different color), Big Beard, Nose-Cut-Off, Dung-Name, Khazar, Stutterer, Drunkard, Wise, Born-in-the-Purple, Pretty Boy, Caulker, The Old Man, and Discount-Fare
Some were in use during the reign. In addition to being frequently disloyal, the Byzantines also had one of the most irreverent imperial cultures.

zh: 这些辱骂形式提供了民众对“帝国理念”反应的片段视图，是街头对宫殿辉煌的回答。人类学家詹姆斯·斯科特（James Scott）写过一部关于颠覆性、往往隐蔽的民众话语方式的有影响力研究，他论证：
en: These forms of abuse provide snippet views of the popular response to the “imperial idea,” the street’s answer to the splendors of the palace. James Scott, an anthropologist who has written an influential study of subversive, often hidden, popular modes of discourse, has argued that:

zh: 在这种情况下可能发展的几乎是一种双重文化：充满光鲜委婉语、沉默与陈词滥调的官方文化，与一种拥有自己历史、自己文学与诗歌、自己尖刻俚语、自己音乐与诗歌、自己幽默、自己对短缺、腐败与不平等之认知的非官方文化——后者可能再次广为人知，却不可引入公共话语。
en: what may develop under such circumstances is virtually a dual culture: the official culture filled with bright euphemisms, silences, and platitudes and an unofficial culture that has its own history, its own literature and poetry, its own biting slang, its own music and poetry, its own humor, its own knowledge of shortages, corruption, and inequalities that may, once again, be widely known but that may not be introduced into public discourse.

zh: 拜占庭高官（无论受欢迎与否）与失败的篡位者也是目标。“君士坦丁堡人在所有社会层面都明显偏好嘲弄……〔它〕是都城政治生活的重要因素，往往作为人民意见的公开表达。”
我们上面看到人民在狄奥多西·莫诺马霍斯流放后为他编小调，佐纳拉斯引了它；小调讥讽他自以为能发动民众，结果徒劳。这反映一种充满活力的民众政治参与文化。但关于相关各朝的大多数现代史书很少提到这些歌，仿佛它们与政治无关——政治是精英与宫殿的事务。鉴于本章呈现的证据，我相信皇帝密切监测这类东西。从性口号到
与“挖出他的骨头！”也许只有一小步。“皇帝与臣民彼此惧怕。”
此外，拜占庭帝国历史上从未有一个时刻臣民不知道其皇帝易受群众行动伤害。坐在皇位上始终如提比略（Tiberius I）最初所描述：抓着狼的耳朵。
en: Byzantine high officials, both popular and unpopular, were also targeted, as were failed usurpers. “The Constantinopolitans, at all social levels, had a distinct predilection for ridicule... [which] was an important factor in the political life of the capital, often serving as the public expression of the people’s opinions.”

We saw above how the people made up a ditty about Theodosios Monomachos after his exile, which Zonaras quotes; it stresses his delusional failure to mobilize public opinion. This reflects a vibrant culture of popular political engagement. But one rarely finds references to these songs in most modern histories of the reigns in question, as if they had nothing to do with politics, the latter being the business of the elite and palace. Given the evidence presented in this chapter, I believe that emperors monitored such things closely. It was perhaps a small step from a sexual slogan to
and Dig up his bones! “Emperors and their subjects feared each other.”

Moreover, there was never a point in the history of the Byzantine empire when subjects did not know that their emperors were vulnerable to mass action. Sitting on the throne was always as Tiberius I had first described it: holding the wolf by the ears.

zh: 民众歌曲被正确地视为欢呼的反面，其历史从罗马到拜占庭连续不断。M. S. 威廉斯（M. S. Williams）论证它们：
en: Popular songs have rightly been seen as the flip-side of acclamations, and their history was continuous from Rome to Byzantium. M. S. Williams argues that they:

zh: 产生一种可导向政治与社会目的的集体“团结与能量”。如此，它们对任何当权者构成潜在威胁，且无论如何那些隐含或明确宣称代表人民统治的人绝不能忽视……一个共同行动、并在此过程中展示力量的群体是不可与之争辩的，它代表了罗马政治与宗教中许多要紧的东西：团结、共同认同、共识，以及最终的权威与正当性。
en: produced a collective “unity and energy” that could be directed toward political and social ends. As such, they represented a potential threat to anyone in authority and, in any case, could certainly not be ignored by those who claimed implicitly or explicitly to govern on behalf of the people... A crowd that acted together, and in the process showed its strength, was not to be argued with, and it represented much that mattered in Roman politics and religion: unity, common identity, consensus, and, ultimately, authority and legitimacy.

zh: 这种民众文化的表演没有单一固定场所，它源于舆论尚未成形、可能不可追溯的根源。但有些场所皇帝试图疏导这种潜在破坏性力量、引导它转为对自己的支持，尤其是赛马场、君士坦丁广场与圣索菲亚大教堂（它往往既作为公共论坛也作为教堂）。我们已看到那些相同地方如何在革命时刻成为焦点。皇帝失去人心时，人民会到当初集体欢呼拥立他的地方将他废黜，
的呼喊如今撤销先前的
。赛马场主要是皇帝试图把舆论赢到自己一边的地方。它也是人民表达不满（关于不受欢迎官员或政策）的地方。这种动态在帝国早期罗马就已存在，但在晚期古代似乎更突出。
一些史家把这些遭遇视为罗马
失去的投票权的替代。
范·努费伦（Van Nuffelen）正确地反对那些把欢呼视为对皇帝效忠的排演性空洞姿态者：“支持的呼喊与侮辱之间无法划出正式区别：两者以相似方式、在相同语境中发出。”
它们对双方都充满风险。
en: There was no one site associated with the performance of this popular culture, which stemmed from the inchoate and probably untraceable roots of public opinion. But there were venues where emperors tried to channel this potentially destructive force and corral it in a supportive direction, especially the hippodrome, the forum of Constantine, and Hagia Sophia (which often acted as much as a public forum as a church). We have seen how those same places could also become focal points in revolutionary moments as well. The people deposed unpopular emperors at the same places where they had collectively acclaimed them, chants of
now canceling out the former

The hippodrome was mostly where emperors tried to win public opinion to their side. It was also where the people made their grievances known, about an unpopular official or policy. This dynamic was in place in early imperial Rome, but it seems to have been more prominent in late antiquity.
Some historians have seen these encounters as surrogates of the lost voting rights of the Roman

Van Nuffelen has rightly objected to those who view acclamations as staged and empty gestures of loyalty to the emperors: “no formal distinction can be drawn between shouts of support and insults: both were voiced in similar ways and identical contexts.”
They were full of risk for both sides.

zh: “皇帝坐在他的包厢里，周围是按序就座的各等级各阶级代表，竞技场确实是罗马国家的缩影”
——或更确切地说，罗马
的缩影。然而我们绝不能犯那个（持续的）错误：把仪式秩序与
混淆，因为前者只反映一种随具体政治形势而定的一套布置，通常只在仪式期间成立，体现安排者的特定利害。若我们想把赛马场视为罗曼尼亚的缩影，可以，但必须记住其有序的仪式规范反映的是帝国对社会秩序的看法，一种一厢情愿。然而赛马场也见证愤怒、骚乱、谈判与暴力，那些时刻反映的倒是帝国秩序的不稳与脆弱。几个世纪后，这个地方仍被查士丁尼屠杀的死者萦绕：关于皇帝把他们的尸体埋在赛马场旁的故事流传开来。
en: “With the emperor in his box, surrounded by representatives of all ranks and classes seated in due order, the circus was indeed a microcosm of the Roman state”
—or, rather, of the Roman
Yet we must not make the (persistent) mistake of confusing ceremonial orders with
for the former reflect only an

arrangement of social orders that obtained under contingent political circumstances, usually in a bracketed ceremonial context. If we want to view the hippodrome as a microcosm of Romanía we can do so, but we must remember that its orderly ceremonial norms reflected an imperial view of the social order, a form of wishful thinking. Yet the hippodrome also witnessed anger, turmoil, negotiations, and violence, and such moments reflected rather the instability and fragility of the imperial order. Centuries later, the place was still haunted by the dead of Justinian’s massacre: stories had emerged about where the emperor had buried their bodies by the hippodrome itself.

zh: 我想以尼基塔斯·科尼亚特斯的一段话结束本节，它常被用来说明精英对君士坦丁堡“暴民”的轻蔑，但从人民主权的观点看其实颇富揭示性。科尼亚特斯当然在有生之年见证人民促成许多政权更迭。谈及1181年事件——人民团结到玛丽亚·科穆宁娜（Maria Komnene）周围、支持她对抗
阿莱克修斯的斗争，并最终把安德罗尼库斯抬上皇位
——他有这样的话：
en: I would like to close this section with a passage from Niketas Choniates that is often used to illustrate the condescending views that the elite had of the Constantinopolitan “mob,” but is actually quite revealing from the viewpoint of popular sovereignty. Choniates had, of course, witnessed the people effect many regime-changes in his lifetime. Referring to the events of 1181, when the people rallied behind Maria Komnene in her struggle against the
Alexios, and ultimately elevated Andronikos to the throne,
he had this to say:

zh: 任何其他城市的全体民众都可能以非理性为乐、一旦下定决心就不可阻挡。但君士坦丁之城的民众是其中最无序的，以冲动为乐、

因为不同背景的人参与其公共生活，它随他们行业的多样而改变思维方式（可以说）。但鉴于最坏的事业总是获胜、在众多酸葡萄中难找一颗熟葡萄，正因如此民众既不理性地推进目标、也不对执行作充分预见；相反，只凭一则传言就能使他们起而反抗，它比火更具破坏性地肆虐……它被指责性格无常、善变是合理的。君士坦丁之城的居民从未被认为做过对自己最有利的事，也未服从过那些提议增进公共利益的人……他们对当局的漠视被视为一种天生之恶。同一个人今天被他们合法宣布为职官，明天就被他们侮辱为罪犯，两种情形都表明他们不知道自己在做什么、缺乏良好判断与温和性情。
en: The entire populace of any other city might be found to rejoice in irrationality and be unstoppable once it has set its mind to something. But that of the City of Constantine is the most disorderly of them all, rejoicing in its impulsiveness and

insofar as people of different backgrounds take part in its public life and it varies its way of thinking, one could say, according to the diversity of their trades. But given that the worst cause always wins and that one can scarcely find a ripe grape among the many sour ones, for this reason the populace neither proceeds to its objectives with reason nor gives adequate forethought to their execution; rather, rumor alone impels it to sedition, and it rages more destructively than fire... Reasonably it has been accused of being afflicted with inconstancy of character and fickleness. The inhabitants of the City of Constantine have never been known to do what was best for themselves nor have they obeyed others who were proposing to benefit the common interest... Their indifference to the authorities has been maintained as an evil innate to them. The same man whom today they legally declare to be a magistrate, the next day they will insult as a malefactor, revealing in both instances that they do not know what they are doing and that they are ignorant of good judgment and moderate temperament.

zh: 这一切真正意味着的只是：科尼亚特斯这样的社会政治精英成员与帝国当局，无法以他们想要的方式预测或控制民众行为。然而民众的“缺乏理性”可能只意味着他们对自己所做之事有自己的理由，而那些理由对精英是不透明的。
这是对我们《拜占庭人民史》的又一瞥。科尼亚特斯沮丧于他及其阶级受制于人民的政治选择。他不否认人民有权以其认为合适的任何方式干预；他只是抱怨他们干预的方式：他们本应更“理性”。他甚至没说他们应安分守己、别碰政治。但民众善变只有在共和（或民主）体制内才是政治问题，在绝对君主制中则不是。科尼亚特斯似乎接受：在这个治理体制内，人民
与
的呼喊塑造了帝国政治史的进程，反映帝国官员声望的变化。也许他希望并非如此，但即便对这一点我们也不要急于下判断。在他对命运之年1203–1204的记述中，科尼亚特斯似乎赞美在政治精英失败时挺身负责的民众：正是他们比任何人都更把面对拉丁侵略、以及本国精英与外敌勾结时的民族利益防卫放在心上。
科尼亚特斯自己的同情与观点，并不比他所蔑视的民众更固定稳定（许多现代学者也未能给他的立场下一个定论）。
en: All this really means is that members of the social and political elite such as Choniates and the imperial authorities could neither predict nor control the behavior of the populace in the way that they would like. The populace’s “lack of reason,” however, may just mean that they had their own reasons for doing what they did, reasons that were opaque to the elite.
This is another glimpse into our

Choniates is frustrated that he and his class were at the mercy of the people’s political choices. He does not deny that they had the right to intervene in whatever way they saw fit; he is merely complaining about the way that they did so: they ought to have been more “reasonable.” He does not even say that they should know their place and stay out of politics. But popular fickleness is a political problem only within republican (or democratic) systems, not in absolute monarchies. Choniates seems to accept that, within this system of governance, the people’s shouts of
and

shaped the course of the empire’s political history, reflecting the changing popularity of imperial officials. Maybe he wished it were otherwise, but let us not rush to judgment even on that. In his account of the fateful year 1203–1204, Choniates seems to praise the populace who took charge at a time when the political elite was failing: it was they who, more than anyone else, took to heart the defense of national interests in the face of Latin aggression and the collusion of their own elite with the foreigners.
Choniates’s own sympathies and views were not any more fixed and stable than those of the populace he scorned (teams of modern scholars have failed to pin him down).

zh: 总之，对皇帝权力的限制不是神学的或法律的：它们是政治—意识形态的，源于共和国以民众拥戴为根基这一事实。皇帝必须在臣民认为可接受的边界内治理，否则自担后果。

children: 正当性就是民众的拥戴。

zh: 这是经由舆论的帝国治理。每位皇帝以不同方式面对这一挑战，没有保证成功的公式。
en: In sum, the limitations on the emperor’s power were not theological or legal: they were political-ideological and stemmed from the populist basis of the republic. Emperors had to govern within the boundaries of what their subjects considered acceptable or risk the consequences.
This was imperial governance by public opinion. Each emperor faced this challenge in a different way, and there was no formula that guaranteed success.

zh: 将政治领域扩展到君士坦丁堡之外
en: Expanding the Political Sphere beyond Constantinople

zh: 共和国限于君士坦丁堡吗？人们假设“政治过程实际上集中于君士坦丁堡。”
正如马格达利诺（Magdalino）简洁所言：拜占庭=君士坦丁堡。
即便倡导共和拜占庭的贝克（Beck），也把行省排除在其论证之外。
但有理由修正这一进路。我们已遇到似乎指涉一个全罗马政治集体的文本。本节将据此勾勒一个把行省罗马人纳入共和国运作的论证。
en: Was the republic limited to Constantinople? It is assumed that “the political process was effectively concentrated in Constantinople.”
As Magdalino has succinctly put it, Byzantium = Constantinople.
Even Beck, who advocated a republican Byzantium, excluded the provinces from his argument.

But there are reasons to revise this approach. We have encountered texts that seemed to refer to a pan-Roman political collective. This section will accordingly outline an argument that would bring provincial Romans into the workings of the republic.

zh: 在提出论证前，我想把注意力拉回刚引的科尼亚特斯段落的第一句。他说的是

拜占庭城市的人民都非理性、不可治理，但都城的最糟。校正其偏见语言后，行省居民在政治中施展意志是一个值得考虑的可能性。但我们面临方法论问题。我们的史料或写于都城、或带君士坦丁堡偏见。其作者是身居高位者，相信写史关乎权力中心发生的最重大事件。他们无意记录普通人的日常生活，对行省政治也一样不感兴趣——除非那些以某种方式影响都城。但这不意味着没有行省政治，正如不意味着普通男女没有日常经验。此外，我所谓行省政治，不是指纯地方意义事务的政治，而是我为君士坦丁堡提出的同一种“参与
”（πολιτεύεσθαι），即参与帝国范围的政治过程。在缺乏可与都城史料相比的史料（都城史料本身也很少详细）的情况下，我们如何论证政治领域遍及帝国（即便承认有些地方比别处稀薄）？共和国限于都城吗？行省舆论算数吗？行省对政治人物声望的感知影响中心政治吗？
en: Before presenting the argument, I would like to draw attention back to the first sentence of the passage from Choniates that was just quoted. What he says is that the people in

Byzantine cities were irrational and ungovernable, but that those of the capital were the worst. Correcting for his biased language, that the provincials exerted their will in politics is a possibility worth considering. But we face a methodological problem. Our sources were written either in the capital or with a Constantinopolitan bias. Their authors were men who had reached high office and believed that the writing of history concerned the most momentous events that transpired at the center of power. They were no more interested in provincial politics than they were in recording the daily experiences of ordinary men and women, unless of course those somehow impacted the capital. But this does not mean that there were no provincial politics any more than it means that average men and women had no day-to-day experiences. By provincial politics, moreover, I do not mean politics about matters of purely local significance but the same kind of “taking part in the

” (πολιτεύεσθαι) that I have proposed for Constantinople, a participation in empirewide political processes. How, in the absence of sources comparable to those that we have for the capital (which are themselves rarely detailed), can we make the case that the political sphere spread across the empire, even if admittedly thinner in some places than others? Was the republic confined to the City? Did provincial public opinion count for anything? Did provincial perceptions of the popularity of political figures affect politics at the center?

zh: 我们可以作一个一般性论证：尽管有君士坦丁堡的势利，
始终被理解为“罗马人的

罗马人的，正如皇帝是所有罗马人的皇帝、不仅都城的。罗曼尼亚共同体不限于一城。然而这一进路面临两个问题。首先，其前提不会被所有人接受。许多史家相信拜占庭人根本不是罗马人（尽管他们自称），或他们只是作为“罗马皇帝”的臣民才是罗马人，因此离皇帝更近者在拜占庭“做罗马人”的游戏中（无论那究竟是什么）作用更大。回应这些异议需要另一卷书。那卷书正与本书同时写作，将处理拜占庭人自己如何感知其罗马认同的同质性与全国范围、以及把都城与行省连成单一社会的多重渠道与联系；但最好在这里避免这条解释路线。第二个问题更务实。即便我们承认罗曼尼亚是一个涵盖所有罗马人（包括行省）的同质政治场域，也不改变其中一些人处境使其比他人更活跃的事实。
概念不能排除大多数罗马人很少参与、很少发言的可能性（事实上是大概率）。他们基本不得不遵守别处作出的决定，即便那是都城
作出的。
en: We could make a general argument and say that, Constantinopolitan snobbery notwithstanding, the
was always understood to be the “
of the Romans,” that is, of

the Romans, just as the emperor was the emperor of all the Romans, not merely those of the capital. The community of Romanía was not limited to one city. This approach, however, faces two problems. First, its premises will not be accepted by everyone. Many historians believe that the Byzantines were not Romans at all, despite what they themselves claimed, or that they were Roman only insofar as they were the subjects of the “Roman emperor,” and therefore that those who were closer to him had a greater role to play in the game of being Roman in Byzantium, whatever exactly that was. To respond to these objections would require another volume. While that is being written alongside the present book and will address the question of how the Byzantines themselves perceived the homogeneity and national scope of their Roman identity as well as the multiple channels and connections that linked the capital and provinces into a single society, it would be best to avoid this line of interpretation here. The second problem is more pragmatic. Even if we grant that Romanía was a homogeneous political field that encompassed all the Romans, including those of the provinces, that does not change the fact that some of them were so situated as to be more active in it than others. The concept of the

cannot preclude the possibility, indeed the likelihood, that most Romans took little part and had little say in it. They basically had to abide by the decisions that were made elsewhere, even if by the
of the capital.

zh: 在评估行省在拜占庭政治中的作用时，我们必须先明确我们在找什么。按动词
的拜占庭含义，任何使人接触共同利益的活动；任何公共行为或社会角色；任何与治理制度（财政、司法、行政或军事）的互动；或仅仅被动地依法律生活，都可被理解为“参与
”。在这方面行省罗马人与都城者地位相同。然而我们找的是一种触及社会共和意识形态核心的参与，即唯有人民同意能使那些治理制度正当。我们已看到都城人民履行此功能的方式。行省罗马人呢？
en: In assessing the provincial role in the politics of Byzantium, we must first specify what we are looking for. According to the Byzantine meaning of the verb

any activity that brought one into contact with the common interests; any public act or social role; any interaction with the institutions of governance, whether fiscal, judicial, administrative, or military; or simply living passively in accordance with the laws could be understood as “taking part in the

” In this respect, provincial Romans were on the same footing as those of the capital. However, we are looking for participation of a kind that goes to the heart of the society’s republican ideology, namely, that only popular consent could make those institutions of governance legitimate. We have seen the ways in which the people of the capital performed this function. What about provincial Romans?

zh: 让我们回想行省生活的一个关键事实。许多觊觎拜占庭皇位的叛乱者在行省起事、一路打到都城，沿途巩固支持与资源。许多成功了，包括福卡斯、希拉克略、提比略三世、查士丁尼二世（705年）、利奥三世、君士坦丁五世（741年反对阿尔塔巴斯多斯，Artabasdos）、尼基弗鲁斯二世·福卡斯、伊萨克一世·科穆宁、尼基弗鲁斯三世·博塔内亚特斯、阿莱克修斯一世·科穆宁、以及（部分）安德罗尼库斯一世·科穆宁。但我们不应把论证限于成功者，因为在被击败前所有叛乱者都经历同样的动作。只考虑完全成形的军事叛乱，不到五分之一的叛乱能推翻在位皇帝，
但这仍远高于（比如说）现代美国国会选举的成功率（那里通常90%以上在任者获胜）。若计入数十次失败的重大起事，则帝国历史全程平均约每十年一次。

这一切对行省居民的政治生活意味着什么？嗯，我们必须做的第一件事是把自己放到叛乱者及其控制领土内人民的处境。我们必须停止把君士坦丁堡的统治者视为“皇帝”、其对手视为“叛乱者”，因为在他自己心中、在其领土内，叛乱者就是“皇帝”。在君士坦丁堡统治的那个才是不正当的。谁决定这种正当与不正当的平衡？叛乱者凭何种正当性来源宣称一个在都城经正式欢呼的皇帝如今不正当、必须被替换？最终基于他自己已被其领土内的罗马人（全是行省居民）欢呼这一事实。
en: Let us recall a crucial fact about provincial life. Many of the rebels who aimed for the throne of Byzantium began their rebellions in the provinces and fought their way to the capital, consolidating support and resources along the way. Many succeeded, including Phokas, Herakleios, Tiberios III, Justinian II (in 705), Leon III, Konstantinos V (against Artabasdos, in 741), Nikephoros II Phokas, Isaakios I Komnenos, Nikephoros III Botaneiates, Alexios I Komnenos, and (in part) Andronikos I Komnenos. But we should not limit the argument to those who succeeded, for, until they were defeated, all rebels went through the same motions. Considering only fully fledged military rebellions, fewer than one in five defeated a sitting emperor,

but this is still a far higher ratio of success than, say, modern congressional elections in the United States (where it is typical for over 90% of incumbents to win). If we include the dozens of major revolts that failed, we have an average of about one per decade over the course of the empire’s history.

What did all this mean for the political life of the provincials? Well, the first thing that we must do is put ourselves in the position of the rebel and the people in the territory he controlled. We must stop regarding the ruler in Constantinople as “the emperor” and his rival as “the rebel,” because in his own mind, and in his territory, the rebel was “the emperor.” It was the one ruling in Constantinople who was illegitimate. Who determined this balance of legitimacy and illegitimacy? On the basis of what source of legitimacy did the rebel claim that an emperor duly acclaimed in the capital was now illegitimate and had to be replaced? Ultimately it was based on the fact that he himself had been acclaimed by the Romans in his territory, all of them provincials.

zh: 在君士坦丁堡使权力正当化的仪式在行省被反复表演。起兵争位的人经欢呼即位，设立宫廷，穿戴罗马皇帝一切标志性的服饰，承担职能并行使权力。他任命高官、治理臣民、以自己名义铸币，
并统率军队。其政权的庆典与等级、以及给他正当性的原则，都镜像君士坦丁堡。行省居民暂时拥有自己的小新罗马。

这几乎在任何地方都能做。意味着至少在一定程度上，所有声望与舆论的政治在受叛乱影响的地区被复制。叛乱者（假定他不是不情愿地被推上皇位主张）已估量过民众情绪。我们上面看到许多叛乱者相信对手缺乏声望会帮自己夺取皇位，而反叛一个受欢迎的皇帝是愚蠢的。但这不仅适用于君士坦丁堡舆论。它是一种往往由叛乱者及其高层在其驻节行省形成、或许首先在那里形成的意见。那么鉴于叛乱之多，行省意见在塑造拜占庭权力分配上起了巨大作用。不仅如此：中心的帝国政策总要应对行省叛乱的
，试图通过为政权赢得善意（即设法争取舆论支持）来预防。这反过来意味着行省罗马人生活在——且
自己生活在——一个紧张的政治环境中，它可能突然要求他们作出与君士坦丁堡人相同的权力分配选择。受叛乱者或潜在叛乱者统治，他们总在考虑选项。他们过的不是非政治的生活。
en: The ceremonies by which power was legitimated in Constantinople were performed repeatedly in the provinces. The rebel-emperor was acclaimed, held court, and took on all the insignia, functions, and powers of a Roman emperor. He appointed men to high office, governed his subjects, issued coins in his own name,

and led his armies. The celebrations and hierarchies of his regime as well as the principles that gave him legitimacy mirrored those of Constantinople. Provincials temporarily had their own little New Romes.

This could be done almost anywhere. It means that, at least to a certain degree, all the politics of popularity and public opinion was replicated in the areas affected by the rebellion. The rebel, assuming that he was not thrust unwillingly into claiming the throne, had gauged popular sentiment. We saw above that many rebels believed that their opponent’s lack of popularity would help them secure the throne, and it would have been foolish to rebel against a popular emperor. But this did not apply only to public opinion in Constantinople. It was an opinion often formed by the rebel and his top men in the provinces where they were stationed, and perhaps formed there in the first instance. Provincial opinion would, then, have played a huge role in shaping the assignment of power in Byzantium, given how many rebellions there were. And not only that: imperial policies at the center would always be contending with the
of provincial rebellions, trying to forestall them by gaining good will for the regime, that is, by playing the game of public opinion. This, in turn, meant that provincial Romans lived—and

that they lived—in a charged political environment that could suddenly require them to make the same choices about the assignment of power as Constantinopolitans did. Governed by rebels or potential rebels, they were always considering their options. They did not live apolitical lives.

zh: 有些限定是必要的。直到1070年代，我们的史料对叛乱者领土内发生的事几乎一无所知。其焦点是他与君士坦丁堡皇帝的交涉、以及他若打到都城城墙时发生的事。换言之，我们没有关于叛乱政权下行省政治的详细记述，可与我们关于政治冲突时期君士坦丁堡的记述相比。因此我们无法测量行省叛乱皇帝欢呼与正当化中胁迫与同意的平衡。后者几乎全是军事总督、拥有军队，他们能够且确实使用那些军队恐吓地方人口、确保欢呼。其中一些可能起初只被军队欢呼，而在君士坦丁堡军队通常不被用来以此方式迫使民众表示同意。但也可能叛乱者是被不满的地方人口推上皇位主张的，后者以与其君士坦丁堡对应者相同的主权精神行动。后者也试图把不情愿的候选人推上皇位，如532年尼卡暴动中他们高呼“拥立普罗布斯为罗曼尼亚的皇帝！”（普罗布斯已明智地逃走）。
en: Some qualifications are in order. Until we reach the 1070s, our sources tell us next to nothing about what happened within a rebel’s territory. Their focus is on his dealings with the emperor in Constantinople and on what happened when he reached the walls of the City, if he made it that far. In other words, we do not have detailed accounts of provincial politics under a rebel regime comparable to the accounts that we have about Constantinople at times of political strife. Therefore, we cannot measure the balance of coercion and consent in the acclamation and legitimation of provincial rebel-emperors. The latter were almost all military governors and had armies, and they could and did use those armies to intimidate the local population and secure an acclamation. Some of them may have been acclaimed only by their army, at least at first, whereas in Constantinople armies were not normally used to extract popular consent in this way. But it is possible also that rebels were pushed to claim the throne by disgruntled local populations acting in the same sovereign spirit as their Constantinopolitan counterparts. The latter too tried to push unwilling candidates to the throne, as when they chanted “Probos for Romanía!” in 532, in the Nika riots (Probos had prudently fled).

zh: 谢内（Cheynet）在其963–1210年叛乱研究中有时指出某起事“被”某城某地区人口“支持”或“反对”，但因史料简略，难以知道这对叛乱者与那些行省居民之间的权力平衡意味着什么。民众不满可能是巨大因素，我们不必假定人们必须被胁迫才加入一个承诺更好事物的叛乱者，正如君士坦丁堡人不必被胁迫——尤其因为他
、且被欢呼为皇帝后立即有权兑现承诺。我们听说行省城市人民起来杀死不受欢迎的地方总督的案例，通常因财政压迫，即便没有任何叛乱在进行。
这表明他们能把事务掌握到自己手中。在适当环境下，这种“憎恨”气候可能有利于一个计划叛乱的野心家。1040年尼科波利斯（Nikopolis）人民被明确这样说到。保加尔人起事发生时他们已把税吏撕成碎片，并加入起事，“与其说是出于对德莱亚诺斯〔保加尔叛乱者〕的爱戴，不如说是因孤儿院院长（Orphanotrophos）的贪婪与对财富的无厌欲望〔此即皇帝之兄约安尼斯〕。”
1066年拉里萨（Larissa）人民与代表地方利益的显要协同行动，起来反对君士坦丁十世、抗议沉重的加税。他们强迫尼库利察斯·德尔菲纳斯（Nikoulitzas Delphinas）接管叛乱指挥，尽管他不情愿。他设法使他们平静，但直到他迫使皇帝作出让步，才平息民众的不满。
en: In his study of the rebellions between 963 and 1210, Cheynet sometimes notes that a revolt was “supported” or “opposed” by the population of this or that city or region, but because of the terse nature of the sources it is difficult to know what this meant for the balance of power between the rebel and those provincials. Popular discontent may have been a huge factor, and we need not suppose that people had to be coerced into joining a rebel who was promising better things any more than Constantinopolitans were, especially since he was

and, being acclaimed an emperor, immediately had the authority to deliver on his promises. We hear of cases where the people of provincial cities rose up and killed their unpopular local governors, usually because of fiscal oppression, even in the absence of any rebellion going on.

This indicates that they could take matters into their own hands. In the right circumstances, such a climate of “hatred” could have benefited an ambitious man planning to rebel. This is explicitly said about the people of Nikopolis in 1040. They had already torn their tax collector limb from limb when the Bulgarian revolt occurred, and they joined it, “not so much out of affection for Deleanos [the Bulgarian rebel] as on account of the Orphanotrophos’s greed and insatiate desire for riches [this was Ioannes, the emperor’s brother].”

In 1066, the people of Larissa, acting in concert with notables representing local interests, rose up against Konstantinos X to protest burdensome tax increases. They forced Nikoulitzas Delphinas to take command of the rebellion, though he was unwilling. He managed to quiet them down, but only after extracting concessions from the emperor.

zh: 我们在凯考梅诺斯（Kekaumenos）那里有对拉里萨短暂叛乱的详细记述，他基于尼库利察斯本人亲笔、交给凯考梅诺斯祖父的报告。它凸显各方在这种情况下必须作的艰难决定。凯考梅诺斯在拜占庭帝国政治作者中罕见地持有行省视角，他把这个故事归在“发现自己卷入叛乱时怎么办”的建议标题下。如我们所见，这在行省是足够常见的经验，尤其在他写作的1070年代。他（给儿子们）的建议是应忠于君士坦丁堡皇帝，但他不得不倡导这一点本身揭示了这一问题实际多么棘手。他建议若别无选择应
加入事业、稍后设法把叛乱者带回正轨，而这正是尼库利察斯声称自己做的（但我们无法知道他那自利版本有多真实）。然而从其记述清楚可见，拉里萨人民在接近他之前已作出叛乱选择，且其不满是财政的。事实上凯考梅诺斯在别处建议行省官员防止税吏压迫，因为那种行为引起叛乱。
在其叙事某处，凯考梅诺斯—尼库利察斯还说“有一条古老的战略法则：凡自愿来到皇帝、叛乱者或将军处者，不应被违背意愿扣留，而应被允许自由回家。”这种“君子协定”的目的似乎是保全皇帝与叛乱者（在其自己眼中也是皇帝）正当性所需的共识之完整。
en: We have a detailed account of the brief Larissa rebellion in Kekaumenos, who based it on a firsthand report written by Nikoulitzas himself and given to Kekaumenos’s grandfather. It highlights the difficult decisions that all parties had to make under these circumstances. Kekaumenos, who is rare among Byzantine writers on imperial politics in that he had a provincial perspective, includes the story under the rubric of advice regarding what to do when you find yourself caught up in a rebellion. As we have seen, this was a common enough experience in the provinces, especially in the 1070s, when he was writing. His advice (to his sons) is that you should stay loyal to the emperor in Constantinople, but the fact that he has to advocate this reveals how precarious the issue really was. He suggests that if you have no choice, you should

to join the cause and try later to bring the rebels back to the fold, and this is what Nikoulitzas claimed to have done (but we cannot know how truthful his self-serving version was). It is clear from his account, however, that the people of Larissa had made the choice to rebel before they approached him and that their grievances were financial. In fact, Kekaumenos elsewhere advises provincial officials to prevent tax-collectors from being oppressive because that type of behavior caused rebellions.

At one point in his narrative, Kekaumenos-Nikoulitzas also says that “there is an ancient law of strategy that he who comes of his own free will to an emperor, a rebel, or a general, should not be held against his will but should be allowed to return to his home freely.” The purpose of this “gentleman’s agreement” seems to have been to preserve the integrity of the consensus that both emperors and rebels (who were also emperors in their own eyes) required for legitimacy.

zh: 这样一个故事只见于凯考梅诺斯、不见于任何史家，引起怀疑：史家可能省略了许多类似事件，即便在连他们通常仅为此类事件写下的一两句简短记事也没有。我们知道更多关于十一世纪后半行省居民叛乱经验是有原因的。除提供行省局部视角的凯考梅诺斯外，我们有两部比此前史书提供更多叛乱细节的历史：阿塔莱亚特斯，因为他既在一个成功篡位者尼基弗鲁斯三世·博塔内亚特斯治下、也为他写作，而其主要对手是其他叛乱者；以及尼基弗鲁斯·布里恩尼奥斯，他基本在写其祖父失败叛乱的英雄记述。它们没提供我们想要的那种细节，但我们可以一瞥底层动态。行省城市人民在作抵抗还是加入叛乱的根本选择时，必须运用判断、行使政治意志。1047年托尔尼克斯叛乱期间，“住在乡间的人尽可能收集当时能找到的补给，挤到都城城门前。”
但马其顿所有城市都以某种方式倒向他一边。例外是赖德斯托斯（Raidestos），它忠于君士坦丁九世。托尔尼克斯从都城撤退时用攻城器械攻击它，但“居民英勇抵抗他。”
阿塔莱亚特斯在赖德斯托斯有产业，提供了那里政治的迷人一瞥：1077年布里恩尼奥斯叛乱期间该城倒向他时，“市民”显然是被说服加入、而非被胁迫。
他们决定的一个主要因素无疑是政权在赖德斯托斯设立的极不受欢迎的粮食垄断。
布里恩尼奥斯向君士坦丁堡进军时，一些城市自愿倒向他，另一些则不。倒向他当然意味着欢呼他为皇帝，事实上宣布不受欢迎的米海尔七世·杜卡斯被废。
1078年叛乱者巴西拉克斯（Basilakes）被击败时逃往塞萨洛尼基（Thessalonike）卫城，但该城人民反对他、站到博塔内亚特斯的将军阿莱克修斯·科穆宁一边。
当阿莱克修斯进军反对博塔内亚特斯时，色雷斯所有城市倒向他——但奥雷斯提亚斯（Orestias）除外。
看到个别城市如何作出支持或反对叛乱者或君士坦丁堡皇帝的不同决定，是有趣的。
en: The fact that a story such as this is recorded only in Kekaumenos and none of the historians raises the suspicion that the historians may have omitted many similar events, even at the level of the brief notice that they usually reserve for them. There is a reason why we know more about the provincials’ experience of rebellions in the second half of the eleventh century. Apart from Kekaumenos, who presents a partial view from the provinces, we have two histories that offer more detail about rebellions than had previous histories: Attaleiates, because he was writing both under and for a successful usurper, Nikephoros III Botaneiates, whose main opponents were other rebels; and Nikephoros Bryennios, who was basically writing a heroic account of his grandfather’s failed rebellion. They do not provide us with the kind of detail that we would like to have, but we can gain a glimpse of the underlying dynamics. The people in provincial cities had to use their judgment and exercise their political will in making the fundamental choice whether to resist or join the rebellion. During the rebellion of Tornikes in 1047, “people who lived in the countryside gathered for themselves as many supplies as they could find under the circumstances and crowded the gates of the City.”

But all the cities of Macedonia had, in one way or another, gone over to his side. The exception was Raidestos, which remained loyal to Konstantinos IX. When Tornikes retreated from the capital he attacked it with siege-engines, but “the inhabitants resisted him valiantly.”

Attaleiates owned property at Raidestos and provides a fascinating glimpse of politics there, when the city went over to Bryennios during his revolt in 1077: “the citizens” were apparently persuaded to join, not coerced.
A major factor in their decision was certainly the hugely unpopular grain monopoly that the regime instituted in Raidestos.

As Bryennios marched toward Constantinople, some cities went over to him willingly, while others did not. Going over to him, of course, meant acclaiming him emperor, in effect proclaiming the unpopular Michael VII Doukas deposed.
When the rebel Basilakes was defeated in 1078, he fled to the citadel of Thessalonike, but the people of that city turned against him and sided with Botaneiates’s general Alexios Komnenos.
When Alexios marched against Botaneiates, all the cities in Thrace went over to him—but not Orestias.
It is interesting to see how individual cities made different decisions for or against the rebel or the emperor in Constantinople.

zh: 史家已关注阿莱克修斯试图说服阿马西亚（Amaseia）城站到他当时效力的皇帝（米海尔七世）一边、并帮助支付赎金以便从突厥人手中赎出起兵反叛的拉丁将领鲁塞利奥斯（Rouselios）。阿莱克修斯召集该城人民的“集会”（ἐκκλησία），请显要捐资。布里恩尼奥斯与安娜（Anna）的平行记述揭示这是一次民众集会，且阿莱克修斯在要钱时更具体地转向显要喊话。πλῆθος（或 λαός）在场但不热衷站阿莱克修斯一边，他必须说服他们。他部分靠把人群转向反对那个少数派——他声称后者从鲁塞利奥斯的叛乱中获益、使阿马西亚人民暴露于危险与报复。
从这个故事大概不可能提取关于阿马西亚可能拥有的任何自治制度的具体信息，更不用说把它们置于从查士丁尼到所谓拜占庭封建化的某种市政委员会
（longue durée）历史中。我难以相信像阿马西亚这样一个军区首府会没有自治制度，毕竟拜占庭连村庄都有手段以集体身份参与法律事务。
对制度史的搜寻会偏离我们这里的目标：即发现行省城市在行省叛乱语境中确有艰难选择要作；这些决定不单由精英作出；且至少在本例中，说服必须作用于舆论才能确保这样或那样的决定。
en: Attention has been paid by historians to Alexios’s attempt to persuade the city of Amaseia to side with the emperor he was then working for (Michael VII) and help to pay the ransom that would release the rebel Latin general Rouselios from Turkish captivity. Alexios convened an “assembly” (ἐκκλησία) of the people of the city and asked the leading men to contribute funds. The parallel accounts in Bryennios and Anna reveal that this was a popular assembly, and that Alexios turned to address the notables more specifically when he had to ask for money. The πλῆθος (or the λαός) were present but were not eager to side with Alexios, and he had to persuade them to do so. He did so in part by turning the crowd against the minority that, he alleged, were benefiting from Rouselios’s rebellion and exposing the people of Amaseia to danger and reprisals.
It is probably impossible to extract from this story concrete information about any institutions of self-governance that Amaseia may have had, far less to situate them in some

history of town councils from Justinian to the alleged feudalization of Byzantium. I find it hard to believe that a place such as Amaseia, a thematic capital, would not have had institutions of self-governance when even villages in Byzantium had the means to represent themselves as legal collectives.

The search for institutional history would divert us from our goal here, which is to find that provincial cities did have hard choices to make in the context of provincial rebellions; that these decisions were not made solely by the elite; and that, at least in this case, persuasion had to act upon public opinion in order to secure a decision one way or the other.

zh: 君士坦丁堡无疑是罗曼尼亚行使民众权力最重要的场所。罗马人的帝国范围
由都城罗马人代表，因为“都城公众是帝国公众的代表性缩影。”
但行省罗马人也有机会在周期性重新分配掌权权的斗争中发声。我们没有像讨论君士坦丁堡那样讨论他们行动的史料。但我们必须思考行省叛乱对那些人意味着什么（无论他们直接煽动还是被卷入），并在一定程度上运用想象。我推测，行省在拒绝承认在位皇帝、欢呼拥立新皇帝时，也会经历和君士坦丁堡相同的过程。我怀疑“拜占庭=君士坦丁堡”等式不会那么牢固成立。只因我们没有那些文学叙事，不意味着事件没发生。
en: Constantinople was far and away the most important site in Romanía for the exercise of popular power. The empirewide
of the Romans was represented by the Romans of the capital, insofar as “the public of the capital was a representative microcosm of the public of the empire.”

But Romans in the provinces also had occasion to make their voices heard in the periodic struggles that reassigned the right to wield power. We do not have sources that discuss their actions as we do for Constantinople. But we have to think about what provincial rebellions entailed for those people, whether they directly instigated them or were caught up in them, and to a certain degree we have to use our imagination. I suspect that the same processes played out there that we see in Constantinople when it came to the repudiation of the current emperor and the acclamation of a new one. I doubt that the equation Byzantium = Constantinople would hold up as firmly. Just because we do not have those literary narratives does not mean that the events did not happen.

zh: 看1070年代之前的事件，阿莫里翁（Amorion）人民似乎在710年代末复杂的入侵与叛乱系列中自行作了决定。
即便斯拉夫人托马斯在君士坦丁堡前被击败后，一些城市仍不接受他们憎恨的米海尔二世——但多数接受了。
恰在同一时间，西西里的罗马人皇帝（即叛乱者）尤菲米乌斯（Euphemios）逼近叙拉古（Syracuse），“进到离城一箭之地，向市民喊话，力图用言辞把他们赢到自己一边。”
这种城墙顶外交如我们所见周期性地在君士坦丁堡前、也在其他卷入此类战争的城市前上演。
尼西亚（Nikaia）主教尼古拉奥斯（Nikolaos）说服其城人民接受安德罗尼库斯·科穆宁，但普鲁萨（Prousa）城抵抗他。
在十二世纪末与十三世纪大部分时间的混乱中，多数城市常得靠自己应付局势。但这并非他们毫无准备的经验。
en: Looking at events before the 1070s, the people of Amorion seem to have made their own decisions in the complicated series of invasions and rebellions in the late 710s.
Even after Thomas the Slav was defeated before Constantinople, some cities would still not accept Michael II, whom they hated—but most did.

At the very same time, Euphemios, emperor of the Romans in Sicily (so a rebel), approached Syracuse, “came to within bow-shot of the city, and addressed the citizens, endeavoring to win them over to his side with his words.”
Such wall-top diplomacy periodically played out before Constantinople, as we have seen, and before other cities caught up in such wars.
Nikolaos, the bishop of Nikaia, persuaded the people of his city to accept Andronikos Komnenos, but the city of Prousa resisted him.

In the chaos of the final years of the twelfth century and for most of the thirteenth, most cities frequently had to fend for themselves. But it was not an experience for which they were entirely unprepared.

zh: 我们也不应在行省的平民居民与拜占庭军队之间作过细区分。在很大程度上，“军队深深扎根于地方社会，从农民社区按地区征募，并在很大程度上由地方人担任军官。”
哈尔登（Haldon）论证，许多参与行省叛乱的士兵必须“首先被视为其社会文化环境所产出的个体”，其次才是有独立团体认同的单位。
那么军区军队部分代表行省人口的利益。叛乱与内战“就不满的来源而言有明确的地方根源。”
我们不应忘记，当拜占庭作者列举
的各组成部分时，军队占有特殊地位，与教会、商人、“人民”及其他整体的假定代表并列。然而另一些时候，军队与人民在含糊术语
中模糊不清，使人难以想象例如谁聚集在赛马场。无论如何，军队作为武装的罗马人民，与君士坦丁堡人民一样有权参与政治过程。他们同样是
的一部分，拥有公认的权利，可以表达意见并介入政事，与人民相同，
尽管他们从未成功违背人民意愿强加一个不受欢迎的皇帝（至少不长久）。
en: We should also not draw too fine a distinction between civilian locals and the Byzantine army in the provinces. To a great degree, “the armies were very much rooted in local society, recruited regionally from peasant communities and officered to a great extent by local men.”

Haldon has argued that many of the soldiers involved in provincial rebellions must be seen “first as individuals produced by their social and cultural environment” and secondarily as units with separate corporate identities.

The thematic armies were, then, partially representative of the interests of the provincial population. Rebellions and civil wars “had clearly localized roots, in respect of the sources of discontent.”
We should not forget that the army held a special place when the component parts of the

were listed by Byzantine authors, along with the Church, merchants, “the people,” and other putative representatives of the whole. At other times, however, army and people are blurred in the ambiguous term

which makes it difficult to visualize who was assembled at the hippodrome, for instance. At any rate, the army, being the Roman people in arms, had just as much a right to participate in the political process as the people of Constantinople. They too were a part of the
with a recognized right to be heard and to intervene, the same as the people,
though they never managed to impose an unpopular emperor against the people’s will, at least not for long.

zh: 一些结论已从本讨论浮现。首先，宣布废黜皇帝、欢呼拥立新皇帝的权利不限于君士坦丁堡人民。它也由巴尔干与安纳托利亚主要路线沿线的罗马人行使。每位皇帝都以普遍共识为目标，因此期望在帝国每个部分被欢呼，无论是他在都城获选、承认他的浪潮由都城向外扩散，还是他从行省进军都城、各地的拥戴也随之传向都城。其次，现有证据无法支持行省政治只由精英操持的观点，这一点和君士坦丁堡相同。即便我们无法重建这些历史，举证责任在于那些否认行省城市“人民”在塑造地方决定、进而塑造帝国历史中起关键且往往主导作用的人。君士坦丁堡的舆论与声望动态在那里以相似方式上演。
en: Some conclusions have already emerged from this discussion. First, the right to declare emperors deposed and acclaim new ones was not limited to the people of Constantinople. It was exercised by Romans along the main Balkan and Anatolian routes too. Every emperor aimed at universal consensus, and so would expect to be acclaimed in every part of the empire, whether the wave of recognition flowed out from the capital (if he was elected there) or from a province to the capital, as he marched on it. Second, the evidence does not support the view that provincial politics consisted solely of elite activity, anymore than it did in Constantinople. Even though we cannot reconstruct these histories, the burden of proof lies on those who would deny that “the people” in provincial cities played a crucial and often a leading role in shaping local decisions and, by extension, imperial history. The Constantinopolitan dynamics of public opinion and popularity played out in similar ways there.

zh: 这些冲突不关乎深层意识形态分歧；没有现代意义的“政党”。它们当然关乎地方利益（通常财政）与人事：谁是为其公民利益统治共和国的最佳人选？人民作此决定的权利不受质疑。叛乱后“很少有人因叛国被处决”，因为目标是“缓解紧张、恢复秩序……把尽可能多的人带回帝国怀抱、说服他们支持皇帝”——我补充：或
皇帝。
多数军事叛乱一年内结束，且没有试图以集体惩罚失败皇帝所有支持者的方式来宣示皇帝职位对

的绝对至上（尼卡暴动是唯一例外、且是部分例外）。皇帝宁愿安抚并拉拢对手的支持者，这再次说明他们在意赢得舆论。惩罚社会大片人群会迅速使政权不受欢迎。只有首要分子被谴责、后来被记为叛徒与得罪上帝受膏者的人，而非可能支持他们的民众。事实上，压制对叛乱民众支持的记忆、把叛乱描绘成一两个狂人的所作所为，完全符合幸存政权的利益，因为否则叙事会事实上质疑政权自身的正当性。维持公众仍然拥护政权这一印象的需要影响了叛乱历史后来如何被讲述。后来的叙事倾向于聚焦少数主导分子而非支持他们的群众。
en: These conflicts were not about deep ideological differences; there were no “political parties” in the modern sense. They were certainly about local interests, usually fiscal, and about personnel: Who was the best man to rule the republic in the interest of its citizens? The right of the people to make this determination was not questioned. “Few people were executed for treason” after rebellions, for the goal was to “diffuse tension, restore order,... bring as many people as possible back into the imperial fold, and convince them to support the emperor”—or the
emperor, I add.

Most military rebellions were over within a year, and there was no attempt to collectively punish all the supporters of a failed emperor in such a way as to assert the absolute supremacy of the imperial office over the

(the Nika riots being the only exception, and a partial one too). Emperors would rather appease and co-opt their rival’s supporters, which again illustrates their concern to win over public opinion. Punishing large segments of society would quickly make the regime unpopular. Only ringleaders were denounced and later remembered as traitors and sinners against God’s anointed, not the populace that may have backed them. In fact, it was entirely in the interests of the regime that survived the challenge to suppress the memory of popular support for the rebellion and to cast it as the act of one or a few deranged men, because otherwise the narrative would effectively call the regime’s own legitimacy into question. The need to retain the perception of public support affected how the history of the rebellions was later told. Later narratives tended to focus on a few leading elements rather than the masses that supported them.

zh: 法外主权与民众的政治化
en: An Extralegal Sovereignty and the Politicization of the Populace

zh: 过去一个世纪学者偶尔愿意断言拜占庭是一种植根于罗马共和主义的混合政体。1924年夏尔·迪尔（Charles Diehl）能写道：“人们熟知那句著名公式：S.P.Q.R.。看来从6世纪末到9世纪末，
（拜占庭元老院与人民）同样曾是一个现实。”
挑战在于识别除欢呼拥立新帝（历来被视为空洞形式）外，还有哪些制度能体现民众的权力。G. 马诺伊洛维奇（G. Manojlović）持与迪尔相似观点，不幸地执迷于赛马场党派，误解其性质、把它们（
）与
）混淆。但他仍把握到罗马人民发挥着关键的“宪制”作用，而且人民自己也明白这一点。
在这方面他是贝克的先驱。但贝克及少数可称其学派者在此事上过于拘泥于形式上的宪制。然而国家制度（宪政理论的积木）在拜占庭属于君主制。问题本应是：皇帝与
的关系是什么？这是一种法外关系，不由制度而由罗马共和主义的底层意识形态（政治的母体）支配。要看到这一点我们必须思考到制度层面之外。
en: During the past century scholars have occasionally been willing to assert that Byzantium was a mixed type of regime with roots in Roman republicanism. In 1924, Charles Diehl could write that “on connaît la formule fameuse: S.P.Q.R. Il semble bien, que, de la fin du VIe à la fin du IXe siècle, le
ait été semblablement un réalité.”

The challenge was to identify the institutions by which popular power was expressed, apart from the acclamation of the new emperor (which was, and still is, regarded as an empty formality). G. Manojlović, who had a view similar to that of Diehl, unfortunately fixated on the hippodrome factions, misunderstanding their nature and confusing them
with the
Still, he grasped that the Roman people had a crucial “constitutional” role to play of which they themselves were aware.

In this he was a forerunner of Beck. But Beck, and the small number of scholars who might be said to be his school in this matter, thought in too-formal constitutionalist terms. State institutions, however, the building blocks of constitutional theory, belonged in Byzantium to the monarchy. The question should rather have been, What was the relationship between the emperor and the

This was an extralegal relationship governed not by institutions but by the underlying ideology of Roman republicanism, the matrix of politics. To see this we have to think beyond the level of institutions.

zh: 政治场域不由制度与领土边界定义，而由从事政治活动的群体构成……在研究此类活动时我们很可能遇到制度。但这些制度应被视为政治过程的实例——一组特定的形式化关系，它们从政治活动中产生、由政治活动构成、并持续通过政治活动被改变。
en: The political field is not defined by institutional and territorial boundaries, but rather is constituted by groups who are engaged in political activity... It may well be that in the study of such activities we encounter institutions. But these institutions should be regarded as instances of political processes—a particular set of formalized relationships that emerge from, are constituted by, and continue to be altered through political activity.

zh: 奥古斯都（Augustus）可能以违反
（祖先习俗）不成文规范的方式把大部分权力揽给自己，但当他一再宣称其权力来自授予他权力的元老院与人民时，他表明接受一条基本共和原则。这一原则作为在
领域运作的意识形态，在拜占庭所有世纪中保持活力，甚至在五世纪中叶后加强。皇帝们自己比任何人都更努力地强化它。
en: Augustus may have arrogated most power to himself in a way that violated the uncodified norms of the

but when he claimed, over and over again, that his power derived from the senate and the people, who had given it to him, he indicated his acceptance of a basic republican principle. This principle, as an ideology operative in the field of
remained alive throughout all the centuries of Byzantium, and was even strengthened after the mid-fifth century. The emperors themselves did more than anyone to strengthen it.

zh: 共和式君主制的框架是稳定的，但每隔几年“人民”（无论都城或行省）就权力转移作出或面临一个选择。没有制度框架容纳这些权力斗争，也不可能有。国家制度早已被
（君主制）主导。但君主制只是
的一个方面、必须从中汲取正当性。
是其制度运作于其中的意识形态语境。这意味着围绕授予或改授
的斗争必然发生在政府制度之外，因此往往暴力。那是拥有一个正当性来自人民同意与人民（或其代表）“选举”的强大君主制的结果，即共和式君主制。欢呼是共和国意识形态与君主制制度之间的接口，反对的呼喊亦然（但方向相反）。
en: The framework of the republican monarchy was stable, but every few years “the people” (whether in the capital or the provinces) made a choice, or faced a choice, regarding the transfer of power. There was no institutional framework to accommodate these struggles for power, nor could there have been. The state institutions had long since been dominated by the
the monarchy. But the monarchy was only one aspect of the
and had to draw its legitimacy from it. The
was the ideological context in which its institutions operated. This meant that struggles over the (re)assignment of the

had, by necessity, to take place outside the institutions of the government, so they were often violent. That was the result of having a strong monarchy whose legitimacy derived from popular consent and “election” by the people (or their representatives), that is, a republican monarchy. Acclamations were the interface between the ideology of the republic and the institutions of the monarchy, as were (but in the opposite direction) cries of disapprobation.

zh: 皇帝行使的权威本来就没有完全确切的法律依据。婉转地说，其权力与法律的关系含糊。较不含糊的是他们与共和国的关系。“问责的语言成为皇帝与曾经主权的
之间持续对话的一部分。必须向他人负责的人，也必须接受对方的批评……公民被鼓励要求其政府问责。”

因此如我在第3章所论，帝国历史在两种可能运作于法律之外的“例外状态”之间摇摆：皇帝的（对共和国负责）与政体其余部分的（只对自己负责）。前者若管理得好，产生相当长的政治社会稳定期，给人皇帝有最终发言权的错觉。就多数实际目的而言他确有，所以我们的历史聚焦皇帝及其政策。后者往往以暴力与无法无天的爆发为特征，就一切实际目的而言是法律的中止。它们打断罗马历史的文本，使各朝与王朝或长或短，引入其间或多或少的突兀过渡。然而这些事件在史料中比在现代史书中更突出。拜占庭叙事更多关于人（个体与“人民”），而我们自己的叙事远更依赖稳定制度（无论其稳定如何被“打断”）。
en: The emperors were not exercising a fully legal authority to begin with. Their power had an ambiguous relation to law, to put it mildly. What was less ambiguous was their relation to the republic. “The language of accountability became a part of the continual dialogue between the emperors and the once-sovereign
Those who are accountable are also subject to criticism from those to whom they answer... citizens were encouraged to hold their government to account.”

Thus, as I argued in Chapter 3, the history of the empire oscillated between two “states of exception” that operated potentially beyond the law: that of the emperor, answerable to the republic, and that of the rest of the polity, answerable only to itself. The first, if managed well, resulted in fairly long periods of political and social stability which can give the illusion that the emperor had the final word. For most practical purposes he did, so our histories focus on emperors and their policies. The second often featured outbursts of violence and lawlessness, for all practical purposes the suspension of law. They punctuated the text of Roman history, making reigns and dynasties longer or shorter, introducing more or less abrupt transitions between them. Yet these episodes appear more prominently in the sources than in modern histories. Byzantine narratives are more about people, both individuals and “the people,” while our own depend to a far greater degree on stable institutions, however “punctuated” their stability.

zh: 革命时期
（法治政体）被中止。那时发生的一些劫掠与清算旧账是机会主义的。
据执事利奥（Leon the Deacon），约安尼斯·齐米斯克斯（Ioannes Tzimiskes）谋杀尼基弗鲁斯二世并如此迅速控制局面，得以颁布法令，宣布劫掠者一律处死。利奥评论说“通常在这种更迭之时，民众中游手好闲与贫困的成员会转向劫掠财产、毁坏房屋，甚至有时谋杀同胞公民。”
有可能民众中某些分子倾向加入篡位或支持政变，因为这给他们机会不受惩罚地劫掠富人宅邸。科尼亚特斯对1201年起义与“胖子”约安尼斯（Ioannes “the Fat”）失败政变的记述暗示了类似东西。
en: In times of revolution, the
was suspended. Some of the looting and settling of scores that occurred then was opportunistic.

According to Leon the Deacon, Ioannes Tzimiskes murdered Nikephoros II and took control of matters so quickly that he managed to proclaim a decree threatening anyone who looted with the death penalty. Leon comments that “usually, at the time of such changes, the idle and indigent members of the populace used to turn to looting property and destroying houses, and even sometimes to murdering their fellow citizens.”

It is possible that elements of the populace were inclined to join in usurpations or support coups because it gave them the opportunity to plunder the mansions of the wealthy with impunity. Something like that is suggested in Choniates’s account of the uprising of 1201 and the failed coup of Ioannes “the Fat.”

zh: 但这种犬儒式的解释只能说明一部分现象。在这种时候，多数暴力或是象征性的、或反映主权人民的正义感（无论由人民自己还是代表他们做出）。例如从

释放囚犯——那个革命套话——事实上撤销了皇帝执法的权威，并可能也释放了他关押的“政治犯”。511年暴力针对一个不受欢迎大臣的宅邸；963年针对布林加斯及其支持者的宅邸；1042年针对所有被认为从米海尔五世政权不公正获益者（包括教堂与修道院）。1057年，安条克牧首狄奥多西（Theodosios）“第一个喊出〔对伊萨克一世·科穆宁的〕认可欢呼，并允许夷平与劫掠那些对正在发生之事不满的高官的宅邸；而他是在那座神圣而著名的教堂内这样做的！”
1181年他们针对都城长官的宅邸等。在一项《人们为何守法》（
）研究中，汤姆·R.·泰勒（Tom R. Tyler）论证人们守法不仅出于理性计算（即避免惩罚或因为符合利益），也因为他们认为那是正确的事。但若他们感知当局正当，就更可能这样认为。换言之，他们关心公平。这可能就是为何当政权被拒斥为不正当时法律崩溃、为何暴力倾向于针对那些从政权不公正获益者。在拜占庭，法律能否通行与当权政权的正当性成正比，而正当性在这里由一种“街头正义”或“人民法庭”衡量。
en: But this cynical interpretation goes only so far. At such times, most of the violence was either symbolic or reflected the Sovereign People’s sense of justice (whether it was done by the people or on their behalf ). Freeing prisoners from the

for instance, that revolutionary cliché, effectively canceled the emperor’s authority to execute the law, and probably freed his “political” prisoners too. In 511 the violence targeted the house of an unpopular minister; in 963 the houses of Bringas and his supporters; in 1042 all who were perceived to have benefited unjustly from the regime of Michael V, including churches and monasteries. In 1057, Theodosios, patriarch of Antioch, “was the first to cry out the acclamation of approval [of Isaakios I Komnenos] and to permit the razing and pillaging of the houses of those high officials who were not pleased with what was happening; and he did it inside that sacred and famous church!”
In 1181, they targeted the house of the City prefect, among others. In a study of

Tom R. Tyler argued that people do not obey the law only out of rational calculation (i.e., to avoid penalties or because it is in their interest) but also because they think it is the right thing to do. But they are more likely to think that if they perceive that the authorities are legitimate. They are, in other words, concerned with fairness. This may be why there was a breakdown of law when the regime was rejected as illegitimate and why the violence tended to target those who had unfairly benefited from the regime. Legality in Byzantium was proportional to the legitimacy of the regime in power, and legitimacy was here measured by a kind of “street justice” or “People’s Court.”

zh: 科尼亚特斯提供了一个代表
中止的形象：劫掠者从长官宅邸拿走公共法典，“其中包含那些关乎所有人（或至少多数人）共同利益的措施；但如今它们在私利贪欲面前无能为力。”
这当然是他的看法，就在我们本章前面考察的他那篇反对君士坦丁堡善变民众的抨击之后一页。但它仍是民众把事务掌握到自己手中时法律中止的有力形象。权力回到真正的主权者手中，由这个具有法外权威的主权者将之授予下一个获得民众拥戴的人。
en: Choniates offers an image that stands for the suspension of the

the looters took away from the prefect’s house the public law codes, “which contained those measures which pertained to the common good of everyone, or at least the majority; but these were powerless now before the craving for private gain.”

This was his view of the matter, of course, coming only a page after his diatribe against the fickle populace of Constantinople that we examined earlier in this chapter. But it is still a potent image for the suspension of law that occurred when the populace took matters into its own hands. Power devolved to the extralegal authority of the true sovereign, to be bestowed upon the next favorite of public opinion.

zh: 这种场景不仅发生在君士坦丁堡，可能也发生在行省：先在叛乱者被拥立为皇帝的城镇，然后沿他向都城的路线（每个城镇决定接受还是拒绝他席卷帝国的“滚动革命”），最后若他打到都城并废黜敌人，也在都城。若叛乱在都城开始并结束，骚乱就限于那里。但鉴于起事与起义之频繁、以及民众需要决定把权力交给谁，许多拜占庭人会亲身熟悉其中的两难。他们会敏锐意识到自己在帝国权力正当化或转移中可扮演的角色。总之，我们必须放弃对这些“臣民”的皇帝中心观——它把他们视为在皇权面前基本驯顺，甚至事实上以他们是否对皇帝“忠诚”来界定其罗马人身份。
我们必须代之以一个模型，承认这种忠诚总是有条件的、这些“罗马共和国公民”（史料中常如此称呼）随时在评估选项、从而行使政治判断、并在关头行使意志。他们中许多可能不想处于那种境地。但他们对此也几乎别无选择。
en: Such scenes transpired not only in Constantinople but probably also in the provinces, first in the town where the rebel was proclaimed and then along his route toward the capital, as each town decided whether to accept or reject his “rolling revolution” sweeping through the empire; and finally in the capital too, if he managed to reach it and dethrone his enemy. If a rebellion began and ended in the capital, the unrest was confined there. But given the frequency of revolts and uprisings, and the need for the population to make choices about the new assignment of power, many Byzantines would have been personally familiar with the dilemmas involved. They would have had an acute sense of the role that they could play in the legitimation or transference of imperial power. In sum, we must abandon the emperor-centric view of these “subjects,” which treats them as largely docile in the face of imperial authority and which goes so far, in fact, as to define their identity as Romans as a function of their “loyalty” to the emperor.

We must replace it with a model that recognizes that this loyalty was always conditional and that these “citizens of the Roman republic” (as they are as often called in the sources) were at all times evaluating their options and so exercising their political judgment and, when it came to it, their will. Many of them may not have wanted to be in that situation. But they too had little choice in the matter.

zh: 我们不应把皇权的暴力转移视为稳定体制里偶发的反常事件。皇帝竭力构造并宣传一套强调稳定的说辞（如我们将在第6章所见），但它从未成功使皇位安全。拜占庭人生活在持续警戒状态中。阿拉伯之春与世界各地（包括西方）的起义，提供了对人民处境的鲜活体会：理论上拥有主权，也深度卷入政治（尽管精英努力恐吓他们或让他们逐渐漠视政事），却几乎没有制度表达意志（正如我们民主选举的骗局日益被揭露）。埃及的事件对拜占庭人会再熟悉不过，包括瘫痪都城的大规模示威、随后人民与军队联盟推翻暴政。就拜占庭而言我们需要把这类事件置于漫长的起义与叛乱历史中。不仅成功者对我们重要，失败者也包含同样的根本选择。事实上我们还必须计入人民决定

行动的所有时刻，因为那些也是政治决定（尽管其数量不可知）。想象它们能给我们拜占庭人政治化程度之感。这就是精英眼中舆论的恐怖。它有时不可预测、能把一切抛入疑问，为一些人打开机会、为另一些人终结生涯（甚至生命）。这也要求我们重审民众欢呼的基调。在现代史书中它们被视为统治阶级应得的、由完全接受“帝国理念”的驯顺被动臣民提供。然而其价值必须鉴于人民能轻易逆转它们、使精英周遭的一切轰然坍塌而重估。任何暴政（即便现代的）都无法长期承受大规模民众抵抗与示威。欢呼是真实的政治资本，但在被重新分配前它能分红多久？即便今天，一张支持某候选人的大规模政治集会照片，看起来可能与一张即将推翻政权的大规模抗议照片无异。
en: We should not regard violent transfers of imperial authority as aberrant moments in an otherwise stable system. The emperors tried hard to develop and project a rhetoric of stability, as we will see in Chapter 6, but it never succeeded in making their throne secure. The Byzantines lived in a constant state of alert. The events of the Arab Spring and the uprisings taking place around the world, including the West, afford a live appreciation of the people’s predicament: theoretically sovereign and extremely politicized (despite the efforts of the elite to cow them or lull them into indifference), albeit with few institutions to express their will (as the sham of our democratic elections is being increasingly exposed). The events in Egypt would have been all too familiar to a Byzantine, including mass demonstrations that paralyze the capital followed by an alliance between the people and army to topple a tyranny. In the case of Byzantium we need to situate such events against a long history of uprisings and rebellions. Not only those that succeeded should matter to us, for the failed ones entailed the same fundamental choices. In fact, we must factor in as well all the times when the people decided

to act, for these were political decisions too, for all that their number is unknowable. Imagining them can give us a sense of the extent of the Byzantines’ politicization. This was the terror of public opinion in the eyes of the elite. It was at times unpredictable and it could throw everything into question, opening opportunities for some while ending careers (and even lives) for others. This also requires us to revisit the tenor of popular acclamations. In modern histories they are treated as owed to the ruling class, provided by docile and passive subjects who fully accepted the “imperial idea.” Their value, however, must be reassessed in light of the ease with which the people could reverse them and bring everything tumbling down about the ears of the elite. No tyranny, not even a modern one, can long withstand massive popular resistance and demonstrations. An acclamation was real political capital, but for how long would it pay dividends before it was reassigned? Even today, the photograph of a mass political rally in favor of a candidate for office can look indistinguishable from that of a mass protest poised to bring down a regime.

zh: 人民能够开启紧急状态，造成“公法与政治事实之间的一个失衡点。”
在拜占庭这种状态就体现为“内战、起义与抵抗”，二者的关系并不限于彼此密切相关。
这就是蒙森（Mommsen）把帝国宪制著名地定义为“受革命合法权利调节的专制”背后的真相，尽管它并不确切是一部宪法、或一种专制，革命也不严格合法。
无论由行省将军还是君士坦丁堡人民发起，
的呼喊给革命以正当性、并标志合法秩序的中止。当合法秩序被中止时唯有真正主权者保持正当，且唯有他——或在本例中
——可重建它。
en: The state of emergency that the people could institute created “a point of imbalance between public law and political fact.”
In Byzantium it actually took the form of, and was not only closely related to, “civil war, insurrection, and resistance.”

This was the truth behind Mommsen’s famous definition of the imperial constitution as an autocracy tempered by the legal right of revolution, though it was not exactly a constitution, or an autocracy, nor was revolution strictly speaking legal.
Whether it was begun by a provincial general or the people of Constantinople, the cry of
gave legitimacy to the revolution and signaled the suspension of lawful order. Only the true sovereign remains legitimate when the lawful order is suspended, and only he—or, in this case,
—may reconstitute it.
